scenes.title: The surveyor's house

beats: Wren comes home to find her old master Edric dead in his chair by the window, peacefully, his last survey of Carrow Fell finished on the table.
She reads his note: the survey must be registered at the Carrow Assize before midsummer, in his name and hers.
A soft-spoken stranger, Gale, calls at the door asking to buy 'the Carrow papers' for the Warden; Wren says there are none and shuts the door.

paragraphs: The door of the surveyor’s house stood open. Wren saw it from the bottom of King’s Stair, where the town dropped away to the harbour in a stack of grey roofs, and she stopped with her hand on the rope of the handcart. Edric never left the door open. He said the salt got in and ate the hinges, and the salt took his knees with it, so the door stayed shut from the first cold morning to the last.

She pulled the cart up the cobbles and left it at the wall. Inside, the hall was dim and smelled of cold ash. His coat hung on its peg. His boots stood beneath it, toes to the wall, the way he always left them.
‘Master?’

Nothing. The kitchen was tidy, the kettle dry, a heel of bread on the board going hard. She went through into the room at the back, the one he called the survey room, where the light came best off the water in the afternoons.

He was in his chair by the window. His head had gone over to one side, resting on the wing of the chair, and his hands lay open in his lap. The window was open two inches, and the evening air moved the grey hair at his temple without waking him. He had the look of a man who had sat down to think and finished thinking.

Wren stood in the doorway a long while. The tide was going out below the town; she could hear it, the long suck and rattle of the shingle. Gulls argued over something on the quay. She had known, in some part of her that kept accounts, that this day would come, and she found that knowing had bought her nothing at all.

She crossed to him and put two fingers against the back of his hand. Cold, and stiffening. She had seen three dead men in her life: her father, a drover crushed at the fair, and the pilot from the *Marrow* who had gone into the water at the harbour mouth. Edric looked less surprised than any of them.

She closed the window. Then she drew the blanket from the back of the other chair and laid it over him to the chin, because the room would be cold by morning and she could not think what else to do with her hands.

On the table under the window lay the survey case, open. The maps were out, weighted at the corners with his brass rules and the lump of haematite he used for a paperweight. Carrow Fell, in his small even hand: the contours of the north side, the old workings, the levels and the shafts, the boundary stones numbered and named. Ink still dark. She touched the corner of the nearest sheet, and it was dry, but only just. He had finished it today.
Beneath the case, folded once, was a sheet of paper with her name on it.
*Wren.*
She read it standing up, because sitting down felt like agreeing to something.

*If you are reading this I have finished the fell, which is the main thing. I have seen the north side now and it is as I thought. The old levels run further than the Crown grant has ever admitted, and the bog above them is no good for grazing and never will be. A dishonest survey would make Vey a rich man and the town a poor one, and I have not made one.*

*Take it to Carrow. The Assize sits at midsummer and will take a survey from a sworn surveyor’s hand, or from his apprentice’s, if she carries his seal and his name. Register it in my name and in yours. It must be done before the Assize rises, or it is a dead paper and any man may redraw the fell to suit himself.*
*You will want to go by the coast road. Do not.*

*I have kept you short of wages these three years and you have never once asked me why. It is because I was buying you the time to finish what I began. That is the whole of your inheritance, and I am sorry for it. You are a better surveyor than I was at forty.*

She read it twice. The second time she heard his voice in it, dry and level, and she had to set it down on the table and stand with her back to the room until she could pick it up again. Then she folded it small and put it inside her jumper, against her ribs, and went to see about the practicalities, because the practicalities were a road she could walk.

There was no money in the house worth the name. There was the seal, in its tin box behind the loose brick in the chimney breast, the brass die worn smooth at the edges from forty years of pressing into wax. There was the survey case, and the maps, and the notes, and the field books going back to the spring. There was Edric, who would need the parson and the coffin-maker and a hole in the ground above the harbour where the wind would get at him. She would do all of it, and she would do it properly, and then she would go to Carrow.
She had just set the kettle on to boil, because the woman from the next house would come soon and there would be tea to make, when the knock came.
It was not the neighbour’s knock. It was three soft taps, unhurried, spaced like a man who had all evening.

Wren opened the door on a man of forty or so in a good grey coat, no mud on him anywhere, his hat in his hand. His hair was going silver at the temples and his face was pleasant in a way that had been practised.
‘Good evening,’ he said. ‘Master Edric’s house?’
‘This is his house.’

‘And you would be the apprentice. Wren Hollis.’ He said it the way a man reads a name off a list he has already checked. ‘My name is Gale. I’m sorry to come at such an hour. I’ve been travelling since noon.’
‘What do you want?’
‘May I?’ He gestured past her, into the hall. ‘It’s a small matter, but it’s better said inside. There’s a wind off the water.’
She did not move. ‘Say it here.’

Gale smiled, and let the smile sit there. ‘I’m told your master kept the Carrow papers. The survey of the fell. I’ve come to buy them, on behalf of Warden Vey, who is prepared to be generous. Very generous, in fact. The Warden has an interest in that country and he would rather have the thing done cleanly than not at all. You’d be paid in gold, tonight, and you’d have my word that nothing further would be asked of you.’
‘There are no Carrow papers,’ Wren said.
His eyes moved once, past her shoulder, into the dim hall, as if he were counting the pegs.
‘Your master was a careful man,’ he said. ‘Careful men keep copies. And careful apprentices know where.’

‘He’s dead,’ Wren said. ‘He died this afternoon in that chair. There’s nothing here to sell you and nothing to copy. If the Warden wants a survey of Carrow Fell he can hire a surveyor, the way anyone else would.’

Something went out of Gale’s face and something else came in, and it took him only a breath. ‘Dead,’ he said. ‘I’m sorry to hear it. He was well thought of.’ He turned his hat over once in his hands. ‘You’ll forgive me if I ask again in the morning. Grief makes people say things they don’t mean, and the offer will still be standing. Gold doesn’t spoil.’ He looked at her a moment longer, mild and patient, and she had the clear sense that he was memorising her: the coat, the boots, the red-brown hair coming loose from its tie. ‘You’ll be staying on here?’
‘I’ll be here to bury him,’ she said, and shut the door, and shot the bolt, which she had never once known Edric to do.
She stood with her palm flat on the wood and listened. Footsteps, unhurried, going down the cobbles towards the quay. Then nothing but the tide.

The kettle began to sing behind her. She went into the survey room, where the blanket-covered shape sat by the window with the last of the light on it. She closed the case, laid the maps and the field books inside in their order, put the seal in the tin box on top, and buckled the straps. Then she sat down on the floor beside the table with the case against her knee, and waited for the neighbour’s knock, and did not sleep.

scenes.title: Fire in the night

beats: Men break into the house in the dark while Wren hides upstairs with the survey case.
In the struggle a lamp is knocked over and the study catches fire; Wren drops the survey case and has to pull it out of the flames.
She escapes through the back garden with the survey case and runs for the river.

paragraphs: The neighbour never came. Wren sat with her back against the table leg and listened for the knock until the tide turned and the water in the harbour went quiet, and what she heard instead, a little after the middle of the night, was the door.

It did not knock. It gave, with a crack of splitting wood that came through the floorboards into her spine, and then there were feet in the hall, two pairs, maybe three, moving without hurry because they did not think anyone was awake to hear them.

She was up before she had decided it, the case in her right hand, her boots already on. The survey room had one door, the one behind her, and the men were between her and it. She did not go through the door. She went the other way, up the back stair that Edric had used to reach the loft where he kept forty years of rolled charts, and on the third step it creaked, and the feet in the hall stopped.
‘Up there,’ a man said, and it was not Gale’s voice. This one was younger and flat, a man who did as he was told and had stopped enjoying it some time ago.

Wren kept going. The loft was dark and smelled of dust and old paper, and she went down on her hands and knees behind a stack of chart tubes with the case pulled in under her chest, and lay still, and the stair creaked under someone climbing it.

Below her, in the survey room, a lamp was lit. She could see the light of it come up through the open trap and lie in a long yellow panel on the loft floor, and she could hear the men moving about in Edric’s room, opening the press, sliding the drawers out, letting them fall.
‘Nothing,’ the flat voice said.
‘Check the chimney.’
A pause. Brick scraped.
‘Nothing. He’d have had the seal in a box. The girl took it.’
‘Then find the girl.’

Boots came back to the stair. Wren lay flat with her cheek on the boards and the case under her ribs and her heart going hard enough that she was certain the boards would carry the sound of it down to them, and the trap door opened wider and the flat-faced man came up with the lamp in his fist, and the light swung across the chart tubes and found her boots.

He did not shout. He came at her across the loft, quick, and got a hand into the collar of her coat, and she drove her elbow back into his throat because it was the only thing free, and he made a wet noise and his grip went slack and the lamp went out of his hand.

It fell. She saw it fall, the flame dragging sideways in the glass, and it hit the floor of the loft and bounced and went down the open trap, and she heard it break below in the survey room, and then she heard the sound that a surveyor’s room makes when fifty years of paper catches at once, a sort of long intake of breath.
The man on the floor was coughing. Wren got up and went down the stair past him, and the survey room at the bottom was already gone.

It had gone in the time it took her to come down twelve steps. The rolled charts along the wall had opened like flowers. The table was alight, the chair where Edric sat was alight, the blanket over him was alight and he was burning in it, and she stood there for one second with her mouth open because there was nothing, there was nothing she could do about any of it, and then she saw that the fire had reached the floor by the door, where she had set the case down when she first heard the door go.

She had carried it down from the loft and put it by her feet without knowing she had done it. It lay on its side against the skirting, and the skirting was burning, and a line of flame was walking along the leather of the case’s near strap.

Wren went down on her knees and took hold of the far strap with her right hand and pulled. The case came half a foot and stopped, wedged against the leg of the burning table. She set her boot against the table leg and shoved it and the table went over with a crash of breaking glass and the case came free, but her left arm had gone down into the gap between the case and the burning skirting to brace it, and when she pulled it back the sleeve of her oilskin was alight from wrist to elbow.

She did not feel it yet. She slapped the sleeve against her thigh twice and the flame on the cloth went out and the fire in the room did not, and she got the case up under her arm and went out through the kitchen, because the hall was full of smoke and men’s voices, and out of the back door into the garden.

The cold hit her arm and then the pain came up it, slow and enormous, from the wrist to the elbow, as if someone had laid a hot iron along the whole length of it and left it there. She knelt in Edric’s bean rows with the case under her knee and got her oilskin off, which took longer than it should have, and the jumper underneath had melted into the burn at the wrist and she had to peel it away from the skin, and when it came away it took the skin with it.

Behind her the house was lighting the garden. Both windows of the survey room were orange, and then the glass went, and the sound of it carried down the hill to the town, which meant that men would come, and that the men who had come already would not want to be found in the garden of a burning house.
She heard them go. Two sets of boots, running, one heavier than the other, off through the gate at the bottom of the plot and away along the shore road.

Wren stood in the bean rows with the case in her right hand and her left arm held out from her body because it did not want to touch anything, and the wind coming off the water found the burn and she had to set her teeth. There was a water butt by the wall. She put her arm in it to the elbow, and the cold took the edge off, and she stood there counting while the fire worked on the roof of the house, and when she took the arm out the whole length of it was a long white blister weeping clear fluid, with the sleeve’s pattern printed red into the top of it.

The case had a spare shirt in it, one of Edric’s, folded in the bottom under the field books. She got it out and tore it into bands with her teeth and her right hand, and she laid the bands over the burn from the wrist to the elbow, and wound them round, and tucked the ends in, and it was not a good job, but it was a job, and the arm would keep.

The town was waking. A light came on in the next house, then another down towards the quay, and a man’s voice called out across the roofs, and the smell of the smoke was going along the street ahead of the fire like a runner with news.

She could not go down to the town. The men would be down there already, or Gale would be, standing at the corner with his hat in his hand and his pleasant face on, waiting for whoever came off the hill with a leather case under her arm. The coast road was the road Gale would watch, and Edric had told her not to use it, and now she understood why he had troubled to write it down.

The river was the other way. The Linn came down off the fells behind the town and went out under the bridge at the quay, and the towpath along the west bank went up into the valley with nobody on it at this hour, and it was the wrong way to Carrow, and it was the only way out of Linmouth that a man in a good coat would not think to stand on.

Wren put the case under her arm, and the arm complained, and she started up the garden to the top gate. Behind her the roof of Edric’s house fell in with a sound like a wave breaking, and the sparks went up over the town, and she did not look back at it, because she had seen three dead men and she had learned that looking back only slowed you down.

scenes.title: Oskar's ferry

beats: At dawn Wren reaches the Linn ferry; Oskar the ferryman grumbles but takes her across for her last coins.
His daughter Pell, nine, chatters to her all the way across and admires Wren's things.
On the far bank Wren sets off east, alone.

paragraphs: The towpath ran with the river all night, and the river ran grey under a grey sky, and by the time the light came up Wren had put four miles between herself and the smoke. She had walked them slowly. The arm had set the pace, and the arm did not want to be hurried.

She had stopped twice. Once at a stile above a sheep fold, where she sat on the crossbar with the case on her knees and listened to the water and heard nothing behind her but water; and once where the path dipped to a shingle bank and she knelt and put the arm in the river up to the elbow and held it there until the cold went past pain and into numbness, which was better. The bandage had come loose in the night and she had wound it back with her teeth. It had bled a little into the cloth, a thin brown line along the inside of the forearm, but not much. Edric's shirt was a good shirt. It had been a good shirt.

She had eaten nothing since the morning before. Her belly had gone past asking and into a flat, quiet state, and she kept accounts in her head to keep from thinking about anything else: four miles from the town, perhaps, at maybe two miles an hour, which was half what she could have walked with two good arms. Daylight at half four, this time of year. The Assize at Carrow rose at midsummer. She could not make the sum come out to anything comfortable, so she stopped making it.

The ferry showed itself as a line across the water, a cable strung between two posts, and under it the flat shape of the punt coming out from the far bank with one figure in it. Wren came down off the path to the landing and stood with the case against her leg and waited.

The ferryman was old and thick through the shoulders, and he brought the punt in with the current and the cable and no particular hurry, and he looked at her the way men on rivers look at anyone walking out of the dawn.
‘Crossing?’
‘Yes.’
‘Where from?’
‘Up the bank.’
He waited. When nothing else came he spat over the side and said, ‘That’s a long walk from up the bank.’ He nodded at the case. ‘And that’s a surveyor’s case, or I’m a bishop.’
‘It’s a surveyor’s case.’
‘Whose?’
Wren thought about it. There was no road behind her and no road ahead of her that a lie would help her on. ‘Master Edric of Linmouth’s.’
The old man’s face did something small. ‘Edric. The one that keeps his door shut.’
‘Kept.’

He looked at her a while longer. He had a broken tooth at the front and grey stubble and the flat pale eyes of a man who had spent sixty years looking at water. Then he put out his hand for the rope and said, ‘Oskar Venn. This is my ferry. There’s no charge for walking on and off it, but there’s a charge for riding, and you’ll be riding. Two coppers.’

Wren got out her purse with her right hand and turned it over into her palm. Two coppers and a broken button. She had had three coppers when Edric died and she had spent one on nothing she could now remember, which was the way of it. She put the two coppers in his hand.

Oskar looked at them and put them in his coat. ‘Get in,’ he said. ‘Stand in the middle and don’t move about. If you go in, I’ll not go after you, because I can’t swim and I’ll not drown for a stranger.’
‘That’s fair,’ Wren said, and got in.

The punt was wet through and had a coil of rope at the bow and a wooden box for a seat, and she did not sit on it because sitting meant bending her arm. She stood in the middle with the case against her shin and her left arm held away from her side, and Oskar put his weight on the cable and the far bank began to come.

Then a head came up over the gunwale from the far end of the punt, where Wren had taken a bundle of tarpaulin for a coil of rope. It was a girl, nine or thereabouts, with her hair in two plaits and a smear of something on her chin, and she looked at Wren with the frank, unhurried interest of a person who has been told to stay quiet and has stayed quiet as long as she could stand.
‘You’re a girl,’ she said.
‘I am.’
‘Papa said we were fetching a man with a case.’ She climbed out from under the tarpaulin, which was not a coil of rope at all. ‘Are you a surveyor?’
‘Apprentice,’ Wren said.
‘What’s the difference?’
‘The surveyor signs. The apprentice carries things.’
‘What things?’
‘Maps. Field books. A chain. Pegs, sometimes, and a level, and a staff to hold it up.’

Pell came along the punt, holding the gunwale, and looked at the case. It was a good case, or it had been: dark leather, brass corners, and along the near strap a blackened welt where the fire had got at it before Wren had pulled it clear. Pell put one finger on the scorch and Wren did not stop her.
‘What happened to it?’
‘There was a fire.’
‘In the night?’
‘In the night.’

‘We saw the light,’ Pell said, matter-of-fact. ‘From the far bank. Papa thought it was the town and I thought it was a star fallen down, and it was neither, it was your fire. Is your master coming after?’
Wren looked out at the water. Grey on grey, going down to the sea behind her with nothing on it. ‘No,’ she said. ‘He’s dead.’
Pell took her finger off the case and stood back a step, and for a moment the two plaits were very still. Then she said, ‘Was he old?’
‘Sixty-eight.’
‘That’s not very old. Old Perrin at the mill is ninety and he still—’
‘Pell,’ Oskar said, without turning round.
‘—he still counts the sacks,’ Pell finished, undeterred. ‘What’s in the case?’
‘Maps of a fell.’
‘What’s a fell?’
‘A hill.’
‘That’s a silly name for a hill.’ She looked at the case again. ‘Have you got a pencil?’
‘In the case.’
‘Can I see it?’

Wren shifted the case against her leg and got the flap up one-handed and took out the field book and opened it at the back, where Edric had kept his pencils in a stitched loop. Three of them, one worn down to a stub, one fresh, one red. Pell looked at them for a long time the way people look at things they have not had.
‘The red one’s for the boundary,’ Wren said. ‘The Crown line and the town line. You mark them red so you can’t miss them when the light’s going.’
‘Why’s the other one so small?’
‘Because he used it for forty years.’

Pell nodded, satisfied with that, and then she saw the arm. Wren had turned a little to hold the field book, and the bandaged forearm had come out from her body, and the girl looked at the bandage and then up at Wren’s face, and she was bold enough to say, ‘What’s wrong with your arm?’
‘I burned it.’
‘Does it hurt?’
‘Yes.’
‘A lot?’
‘Yes,’ Wren said. ‘A lot.’
Pell considered this. Then she reached into her coat pocket and brought out a lump of hard grey bread, no bigger than a fist, and held it up. ‘You can have half. I already had the corner.’

Wren looked at the bread and then at the girl’s face, which had no pity in it, only the arithmetic of a person who has done a sum and got an answer. She took it. It was the best thing that had happened to her since the door gave way.
‘Thank you,’ she said, and ate it slowly while the far bank came up under the punt, and it was dry and tasted of the pocket it had lived in, and she could not remember a meal she had liked better.

The bank came alongside and Oskar took the cable in his fist and brought the punt round with his shoulder, and the boards grated on the stones. He stepped off first and held the rope, and said, ‘Mind the step. There’s a step.’

Wren climbed out. Her legs had gone stiff from standing, and the arm had stiffened with them, and for the first few paces she walked like an old woman. The far bank was the same as the near one: reeds, a track, a low stone wall running up the valley, and beyond it the fells going up into a grey nothing where the cloud had come down to meet them.
‘Where are you for?’ Oskar said. He had the rope over his shoulder and was looking at the track.
‘Carrow.’
He grunted. ‘That’s the wrong side of the water for Carrow. Carrow’s east and south. You’re west and north.’
‘I know it.’

‘Then you know it’s a hundred mile round by the bridge at Harrowgate and forty by the coast road, and you’re not going by the coast road or you’d not be standing on my stones.’ He looked at her flatly. ‘That’s your business. I’ll not ask it. There’s a track up the valley and it meets the salt road above the falls, and the salt road goes to Harrowgate, and Harrowgate is not Carrow, but it’s the right end of the country.’
‘The salt road,’ Wren said.
‘The salt road.’ He shifted the rope. ‘It’s a road for carts and men with mules. You’ll meet them. They’ll not trouble you if you keep to the day.’

She looked back once, across the water, at the town on the east bank. In the grey light it was only roofs and one grey thread of smoke going straight up from the burned house, standing over it like a mast. No one on the quay. No one on the bridge. Whatever Gale was doing this morning, he was doing it somewhere she could not see.
‘Papa,’ Pell said. ‘Ask her the thing.’
Oskar did not ask the thing.

‘The thing about the market,’ Pell said, and when her father still said nothing she turned to Wren and said it herself. ‘When you get to the market. There’s a man at Harrowgate sells glass beads. Blue ones. I saw them at the fair once. They’re not worth anything, Papa says, and that’s why I can’t have one, but I want one anyway.’
‘Pell,’ Oskar said.
‘I’m only saying.’

Wren looked at the girl. Nine years old, barefoot on wet boards, and the one want in her whole small life was a blue bead that was not worth anything. Wren had no money. Wren had a burn and a case and a dead man’s name to carry, and she did not know if she would ever see Harrowgate, let alone come back down this valley to the ferry.
‘I’ll bring you one,’ she said.
Pell’s face did not change much. She was too old for that, or too careful. ‘When?’
‘When I come back this way. It might be a while.’
‘How long’s a while?’
‘Long enough that you’ll have grown out of wanting it. But I’ll bring it anyway.’
Pell thought about this and decided it was a promise, and a promise from a stranger was a real thing, and she nodded once, hard, the way you nod when you are putting something away to keep.
‘East is that way,’ Oskar said, and pointed up the track.

Wren put the case under her arm and started up the bank. The track was wet and stony and it went between the reeds and then up through a gate in the wall, and behind her she heard the cable creak as Oskar put his weight on it, taking his ferry back across the grey water with his daughter in it, and she did not turn round to watch them go.

scenes.title: The horse fair

beats: At the horse fair at Fallow Cross Wren sells her grandfather’s watch and buys a horse.
A drover, Ash Penrose, helps her bargain, and offers to let her travel with his cattle as far as Harrowgate.
They set out together on the Drove Road.

paragraphs: The salt road ran north-west for a day and a half before it bent east, and by the second evening Wren had come down out of the cloud into a country of low green hills with hedges on them, and a smell in the air of animals and woodsmoke and something frying, and lights. She had slept the first night in a shepherd's hut with the door wedged and the case against her back, and eaten nothing, and the second morning her arm had begun to smell sweet under the bandage, which frightened her more than the men had. She rewound it in a stream with her teeth and a clean strip from the tail of Edric's shirt, and by the time she saw the smoke of Fallow Cross she was light-headed enough that the whole valley seemed to tilt.

The horse fair was on the green outside the village, and it was the loudest thing Wren had ever stood in. Cattle bellowed in pens, geese went in a flapping knot down the middle of everything, a man with a bell called out lots, and under all of it the crowd noise rolled like water over stones. Wren stood at the edge with the case between her boots and counted what she had, which was one broken button, and then counted it again, which did not help.
On the third finger of her right hand she was wearing her grandfather's watch.

It was a big silver thing with a worn bow and a scratch across the case where he had dropped it on the cobbles at Linmouth fair the year before he died. She had wound it every day for eight years. She knew its weight, and its tick, which was loud enough to hear in a quiet room, and which she had heard under her pillow for most of her life.
She walked into the fair and found the man with the stall of clocks and knives and rings, and stood in front of him until he looked up.
‘What will you give me for this?’
He took it, opened it, held it to his ear, and made a face like a man tasting milk. ‘Linmouth work. Silver plate. It wants a new mainspring, hear that?’
‘I hear it. What will you give me?’
‘Three shillings.’
‘It's worth six. It's worth six to a man who can put a spring in it and sell it in Harrowgate for twelve.’
The stallholder looked at her more carefully. ‘Four.’
‘Five, and I keep the chain.’

‘Five,’ he said, and counted it out, and she took the money and the chain and walked away with the tick gone out of her life. She did not look back at the stall. She folded the chain into her purse with the button, and her hand was steady, and she told herself that Grandfather had been dead nine years and had never once, in all that time, needed to know what time it was.

The horse lines were at the far end, past the pens, where the smell was strong and honest and the ground had been trampled to soup. Wren had never bought a horse. She had ridden the surveyor's old cob twice a year to the out-farms and otherwise walked. She stood a little way off and watched the dealers work, and tried to learn the trade from the outside of it, and felt the money in her fist going damp.

The mare was on the end of a line of six, tied to a rail, and nobody was looking at her. She was a dun, the colour of weak tea, with a black mane and a black stripe down her spine and black legs, and she stood with her head low and her hip cocked, and when Wren came near she turned her head and looked at her out of one eye with no particular interest, which Wren found restful.
‘Don't,’ said a voice behind her. ‘That one's got a leg like a gatepost and the man knows it.’

Wren turned. The man was tall and rangy, brown from the sun, wearing a coat that had been mended in several places with thread of several colours. He had a stick over his shoulder with a knot in it and he was smiling at the mare rather than at Wren.
‘Which leg?’

‘Near hind. Watch her shift her weight. She's not lame, she's just got no foot under her, and on the moor road you'll feel every stone of it.’ He tipped his head at the dealer. ‘He'll ask twelve and take eight and it's worth five, and if you want a horse to get you to Harrowgate you want the grey at the end with the white nose and you want to pay six for it and not a penny more.’
‘I've five,’ Wren said.

‘Then you want the dun and you want to pay four.’ He grinned. ‘I'm Ash Penrose. I'm taking ninety head up the drove road tomorrow, and I've been in this field since dawn, and I know every horse in it better than the men selling them, which is a low thing to say about a man's own horses but it's true.’
‘Wren Hollis.’
‘Surveyor?’
‘Yes.’

‘Thought so. Nobody else carries a box like that.’ He nodded at the case. ‘And nobody else stands in a horse field looking at the animals like they're a page of figures. Come on. I'll do the talking. You keep your money in your fist and don't open it till I say.’

The dealer wanted eleven. Ash talked about the mare's near hind, and the state of the drove road past Harrowgate, and the price of hay at Fallow Cross in a wet year, and the dealer talked about the mare's breeding and her temper and her way with a gate. Wren stood with her fist closed and listened, and once, when the dealer looked at her to see if she was softening, she said, ‘Four,’ and nothing else, and the dealer threw up his hands and took it.

‘There,’ Ash said, as she counted the coins into the man's palm. ‘Four pound and she's yours and she's sound enough for the road, and if she's not I'll eat my hat, which I have done once before on a wager and it is not a good hat.’

Wren put her hand on the mare's neck. The coat was warm and dusty and the animal leaned into the touch a little, and Wren stood there a moment with her burned arm held away and her good hand on the horse, and something in her chest that had been braced since the door gave way let go by one notch.
‘What's her name?’ Ash said.
‘She hasn't got one.’
‘Everything's got a name. What'll you call her?’
Wren looked at the black mane, the black legs, the dust in the coat. By the gate of the field there was a stand of thistles, grey-green and spined, growing out of the mud where nothing else would.
‘Thistle,’ she said.
Ash laughed. ‘That'll do. That'll do fine. She'll live up to it, I shouldn't wonder.’

She bought a halter and a nosebag with the last of the change, and Ash showed her how to check the mare's feet, and told her about the ford at Cauldwell and the toll at the bridge and the inn at Drake's Bottom where the meat was bad, and then he said, as if it were the smallest thing in the world:
‘Where are you bound?’
‘Harrowgate. Then Carrow.’
‘Carrow.’ He scratched his jaw. ‘That's a fortnight of walking past Harrowgate, and there's no decent road. You're going to Carrow with that box?’
‘Yes.’
He looked at her a moment. He was not a subtle man, but he was not a stupid one either, and Wren watched him decide not to ask, which she was grateful for.

‘Well,’ he said. ‘I'm taking ninety head up the drove road as far as Harrowgate, and I've two men and a boy and a dog, and the cattle go at a walking pace, and there's a place by the fire at night that nobody's using. You'd be company. Also you can count, which Tom cannot, and I have to count ninety head about forty times a day, and it is slowly killing me.’
Wren thought about it. Two men and a boy and a dog, and a road full of drovers and carts, and the country opening green and bright around her, and a hundred miles of it with company.
‘I've nothing to pay you with,’ she said.

‘Did I ask you for money? I asked you to count cows.’ He held out his hand, and she shook it, and his grip was warm and dry and only a little too hard. ‘We go at first light. Bring your horse and your box and a thick head, because Tom sings.’

They set out in the morning with the mist still lying in the bottoms, ninety cattle strung out along the drove road with their heads down and their breath going up pale in the cold, the dog working the stragglers, Tom singing something about a girl from Marrow, and Ash Penrose walking at the front with his stick over his shoulder and his hat on the back of his head.

Wren rode Thistle at the tail of the herd with the case strapped across her back, and the sun came up over the beech woods on the right-hand side, and the road ahead was wide and pale and went on and on, and for the first time since the door gave way she was not afraid of anything that was behind her. Her arm still hurt. Her grandfather's watch was in a stranger's pocket in Fallow Cross. But she had a horse, and a road, and ninety cows to count, and a case on her back with a dead man's name on the seal, and the day was bright, and she counted the cattle twice before noon, and got the same number both times.

scenes.title: Goose grease

beats: A long day behind the cattle on the Drove Road.
Ash dresses Wren's burn with goose grease and clean linen.
She tells him she is a surveyor’s apprentice, but not what she carries.

paragraphs: By noon the mist had burned off the bottoms and the drove road ran pale and dry between the beech woods, and the cattle had settled into the walk, heads down, tails swinging, the herd strung out a quarter mile from the lead beast to the last.
Wren counted them at the bridge and counted them again at the crossroads and got ninety both times, and Ash, walking back along the line to check a lame heifer, took his hat off and waved it at her.
‘Ninety,’ she said.

‘Ninety. Tom had eighty-six this morning and swore blind we'd lost four and I was a murderer.’ He fell in beside Thistle, matching the mare's plod. ‘He can't count past sixty without taking his boots off, and then he counts his boots. How's the arm?’
‘It's all right.’
‘You've been holding it off your side since Fallow Cross like it's got a wasp on it.’

Wren said nothing. The arm had stopped being a thing she could ignore somewhere on the second day, and now it had its own weather: a hot pull from wrist to elbow, worse in the sun, and under the bandage a smell she had first met in a shepherd's hut and did not want to meet again.

They walked on. The road climbed a little and came out of the beeches onto open ground, and the whole valley opened up below them, green and hazy, with the river a thread of light at the bottom of it and larks going up out of the grass like thrown stones.
‘We'll stop at the spring,’ Ash said. ‘The beasts want water and I want to sit down, and you want that arm looked at, whether you like it or not.’
‘It's fine.’
‘You said that at Fallow Cross and then you went the colour of a dishcloth.’
‘I'd been three days without food.’

‘Aye, and now you've had three days with it and you're still grey about the gills. Spring.’ He tapped his stick on the road, twice, like a man closing an argument. ‘I've a pot of goose grease in the bag. My mother swore by it. She'd grease anything that stood still long enough. Said it drew the heat out.’

The spring came up out of a bank of moss on the left of the road, cold and clear, with a stone trough the drovers had worn smooth. The cattle went down to it in a shuffle of horns and tails, and the dog lay flat in the shade with its tongue out, and Tom took the boy off to look for mushrooms with a great deal of instruction and no expectation of success.

Wren got down off Thistle slowly, because getting down was worse than getting up, and sat on the edge of the trough with her boots in the grass. Ash fetched the pot from his bag, and a fold of linen that had been laundered and folded square, and set them on the stone between them.
‘Off with the coat,’ he said.

She took the oilskin off and laid it over the trough, and then she worked the jumper up over her head, careful, because the left sleeve had melted and peeled back from the wrist and anything that touched it made her jaw ache. Underneath, Edric's shirt was wound from wrist to elbow in bands gone stiff and yellow at the edges.
Ash looked at it a while and didn't say anything, which she had not expected.
‘You'll want water,’ he said at last. ‘Hot as you can stand it.’

He took the kettle off the fire the boy had built and poured into a basin, and Wren unwound the bands herself because she wanted to know what was under them. The linen came away in places, and stuck in others, and she had to soak it loose in the basin a strip at a time. Underneath, the burn ran from her wrist to her elbow in one long stripe, blistered white and red at the edges, weeping clear fluid, and printed across the raw flesh was the pattern of the sleeve she had been wearing when she braced the case against the burning skirting: a band of little flowers, red on white.

Ash bent over it with the pot. ‘That's a shirt cuff,’ he said. ‘Look. That's the pattern of it, burned in. I've seen that on a man's back where the fire went through his coat, and it stays. It'll fade, but it'll be a while.’
‘It doesn't hurt as much as it did.’

‘That's not the same as it being all right.’ He dipped two fingers in the grease and set to work, and his hands were big and the grease was yellow and smelled of the farmyard, and he did it the way a man does a job he's done before: a thin coat over the whole of it, no fuss, no dabbing. Wren held her arm out and watched the larks over the valley and did not look at it. It hurt. She had known it would.

‘There's a thing my mother did,’ Ash said, working down towards the wrist, ‘for a burn. You take a raw egg and you beat it up in a cup and you—’ He stopped. ‘No. That was for something else. Forget it. Grease is the thing.’
‘You've done this before.’

‘I've done every fool thing there is. Drovers get burned, cattle get burned, I got burned at Drake's Bottom when I was twenty from a fire that was nothing to do with me and everything to do with a girl, and I'll not go into it.’ He laid the clean linen on, band by band, from the wrist up, and tied the last one off at the elbow, not tight. ‘There. That'll do till tomorrow. Tomorrow we do it again. Every day till it's closed, and if it smells sweet you tell me, because that's the thing that kills people, not the burn.’
Wren pulled the jumper back on, left arm first, and the fresh grease and linen felt cool for the first time in days.
‘Thank you,’ she said.
‘You can pay me in cows.’ He screwed the lid back on the pot. ‘You're a cool one, though. Most people would have said something about that arm before now.’
‘There was nothing to say.’
‘There's usually something.’ He sat back on his heels and looked at the herd, doing his own count without moving his lips, and got ninety. ‘You said Harrowgate, then Carrow. What's at Carrow?’
Wren thought about the case sitting in the shade of the trough with the strap across it, and the seal inside it, and the name cut into the seal.
‘The Assize sits there,’ she said. ‘In the summer. I've a thing to register.’
‘A thing.’

‘A survey. I'm a surveyor's apprentice.’ She said it plainly, because it was true and because it was the part of the truth she could give away. ‘My master trained me six years. Levels, boundaries, drains, the run of the water. I can take a sight through a level and set a mark and write it down so another man can find it in ten years.’
Ash raised his eyebrows. ‘That's a trade. I thought you were a lady's maid run off, or a schoolteacher, or a widow.’
‘I'm not a widow.’

‘No,’ he said, and had the grace not to ask it. He stood up and brushed his knees. ‘Well. Six years' training and you can count, and you've a horse that would follow a cart into a river if you asked her, which is more than I can say for Tom.’ He looked down the road, north, where it went along the shoulder of the hill and out of sight into the next valley. ‘We'll be at Drake's Bottom the day after tomorrow. Meat's bad. Don't eat the meat. There's a woman there makes a barley broth that's worth the walk on its own, and a smith who'll shoe that mare for a shilling if you tell him I sent you.’
‘I've no shilling.’
‘Then tell him I sent you and owe me one.’ He shouldered his stick. ‘Come on. If we sit here much longer the beasts'll lie down and we'll never get them up.’

Wren got to her feet and put her good hand on Thistle's neck. The mare had her head down in the trough and one ear back, listening, the way she did. Ahead of them the drove road went on over the shoulder of the hill, and beyond that the next valley, and beyond that Harrowgate and its wall and its market and its blue glass beads, and beyond that Carrow, which was still a fortnight off and did not know she was coming.
She gathered the reins and swung up, and the arm pulled, and she let it pull.
‘Ninety,’ she said.
‘Ninety,’ Ash said, and went back up the line to shout at the dog.

scenes.title: The bothy

beats: They shelter in a stone bothy; the cattle settle outside.
Ash asks straight out why men burned her master's house.
Wren decides to trust him.

paragraphs: They made eight miles by dusk, and the road came down off the shoulder into a fold of the hills where a stone bothy stood against a bank, roofed with turf, its door half off the hinge. Ash sent Tom and the boy up the valley with the dog to hold the herd on the flat grass by the stream, and Tom went with his boots on his feet and his hand on the boy's shoulder, counting the cattle out loud and getting eighty-seven.
'He'll count them all night,' Ash said. He pulled the door back and looked in. 'It's dry. That's all I ask of a house.'

Wren unsaddled Thistle and rubbed her down with a twist of grass, and the mare put her head down and went to work on the grazing with the rest of the herd, one ear back the way she always had it. The cattle were settling along the water, complaining to each other, and the sound of them was a low noise like a room full of people talking quietly, which was, Wren thought, the nearest thing to a room full of people she had had for four days.

Ash got a fire going in the bothy's hearth with dried cow dung and a handful of dead broom, and the smoke found its way out through a gap in the turf and left the rest of it to them. There was a stone bench along one wall and a heap of old bracken in the corner, and the bothy smelled of sheep and soot and, faintly, of rain that had come through a long time ago and dried.

They ate hard bread and cold bacon that Ash had in a cloth, and he passed her the water bottle and she drank, and for a while neither of them said anything. The fire took properly and the light of it went up the walls and made the stones look warm, which they were not.
Ash leaned back against the bench with his boots crossed and looked at the fire, and then he looked at her.
'Right,' he said. 'I'll ask it now, while we're sat, because I've been not asking it all day and it's wearing on me. Why did men burn your master's house?'

Wren had the water bottle in her good hand. She set it down on the bench beside her, and she took her time about it, because she had known the question was coming since the spring, and she had been deciding.

She had told Pell that Edric was dead. She had told Oskar the case was Edric of Linmouth's. She had told Ash she was a surveyor's apprentice bound for Carrow to register a survey. None of it was a lie, and all of it was a wall with the door left out.

She thought about what a lie cost and what the truth cost, and she thought about the road ahead, and that she had a burned arm and a dun mare and no money, and that if she was going to be carrying this thing a hundred miles into the Warden's own country she would rather carry it with one person on the road who knew what it was.
'Because of what's in the case,' she said.
Ash didn't move. He kept looking at the fire.
'Go on,' he said.

'My master was Edric Rone. He surveyed for thirty years in the western fells, and the last thing he did, the last thing he ever put ink to, was Carrow Fell. The whole fell, top to bottom, every boundary, every drain, every level. He finished it the afternoon he died.' She stopped, and made herself say it plainly, because plainly was the only way she knew. 'The old levels on the north side run further than the Crown grant admits. There's silver under that ground. Workings, old ones, gone over and forgot, and the grant that Warden Vey holds says the mineral rights stop at the beck. They don't stop at the beck. They run a mile and a half past it, under the best of the fell.'
The fire cracked and settled.

'Vey wants the land,' she said. 'He's been buying up the freeholds round the bottom of the fell for two years. If he has the grant as it stands, he has the beck and the bad ground and nothing under it. If the survey goes unregistered, he can swear his own survey at the Assize and nobody's there to say different, and he takes the fell and the town under it goes to begging. If it's registered in Edric's name and mine before the Assize rises, the levels are on the record and the Crown has them, and he can't.'
Ash was quiet a moment. Then he said, 'And a man came to the door for it.'

'Before the fire. He offered gold. I told him there were no Carrow papers and my master was dead.' She looked at her bandaged arm, at the linen, at the ends of the strips where Ash had tied them off. 'They came back after midnight and didn't knock.'
'And the seal,' Ash said. 'You said a seal.'

'Edric's seal. It's in the case.' She hadn't told him that. She didn't know how he had it, except that he had been listening the whole way and putting things where they went, the way drovers do. 'A survey isn't sworn without the seal of the man who made it.'
'He's dead,' Ash said. Not unkindly. Just putting it where it went.

'It's registered in his name and mine,' Wren said. 'That was his instruction. I can swear what he surveyed and I can sign it, and the seal proves it's his work and not mine. That's how it's done. That's how it's always been done.'
Ash uncrossed his boots and sat forward, and picked up a stick of broom and pushed the ends of it into the fire, one by one, watching them catch.
'So the Warden's men are on the coast road,' he said. 'And on the river, likely. And you came the wrong way round, over the tops, to Fallow Cross, and bought a horse off a man you'd never met.'
'Yes.'
'And now you're on the drove road with ninety head of cattle and a drover who talks too much.'
'Yes,' Wren said.
Ash laughed, one short breath of it, and rubbed his face.
'Well,' he said. 'That's a thing to be carrying.'

He looked at her then, properly, and she made herself look back. She had seen men decide things about her before, at the door, at the horse lines, and there was nothing to do but let them do it and be ready.
'You want me to say nothing,' he said.
'I want you to say nothing.'
'To Tom? To the boy?'

'To anyone. Ever.' She said it flat. 'If it gets said in Drake's Bottom it's said in Harrowgate by the week after, and they'd be waiting at the gate. I'm not asking you to lie for me. I'm asking you not to say it at all.'

Ash turned the last stick of broom in the fire and let it burn down. Outside, one of the cattle lowed, and another answered it, and the stream went on over the stones the way it had been going on all evening.

'When I was twenty,' he said, 'at Drake's Bottom, there was a fire. I told you it was nothing to do with me and everything to do with a girl, and I'll not go into it, but I'll tell you the end of it, which is that a man there swore up and down I'd set it, and for three years after, every road I took, someone had heard it before me. There's no such thing as a thing that stays where you said it.' He looked at her. 'So when I say I'll not say it, I mean I'll not say it, and you can stop looking at me like I'm a door you're waiting to hear give.'
Wren let out a breath, and it came out uneven, and she was too tired to be ashamed of it.
'All right,' she said.

'All right.' He stood up and went to the door and stood in it a while, looking out at the herd, doing his count with his lips still, and came back in and sat down and pulled the bracken over toward the fire. 'We'll be at Drake's Bottom day after tomorrow. Smith's name is Reuben. Tell him I sent you and he'll do the mare for a shilling and put it on my slate, and he'll not ask you a question, because he owes me and he knows it.' He lay back on the bracken with his hat over his face. 'Tomorrow we do the arm again. Sleep on the far side of the fire. You'll be warmer and I'll not roll on you.'
Wren lay down with her back to the wall and the case under her head, the strap in her hand, and the fire on her face, and the cattle talking to each other out along the water.

scenes.title: Haldon Bridge

beats: At Haldon Bridge old Mother Agate demands a toll for each beast and each rider.
Ash pays for the cattle; Wren has no coin left.
They cross the bridge.

paragraphs: They came to Haldon Bridge in the afternoon of the fifth day, and the herd smelled the water before they saw it.

The bridge was old, three arches of grey stone with a parapet worn round as a rope at the top, and the river went under it brown and quick with the spring melt. On the far side the Drove Road climbed between thorn hedges and was gone. On the near side, where the road narrowed to the width of the bridge itself, a woman sat on a stool with a stick across her knees.
Ash rode up at the head of the herd and stopped, and the cattle bunched behind him and began to press, and the dog came round the flank of them with its belly to the grass.
'Morning, Agate,' Ash said.

The old woman did not get up. She was seventy if she was a day, wrapped in a man's coat gone the colour of the road, and her hands on the stick were knotted at every joint. She looked past Ash at the herd, and she counted with her eyes, and she did not hurry about it.
'Penrose,' she said. 'You've got more than last year.'
'Four more.'
'Four more toll.'
'That's the way of it.'
'It is,' Mother Agate said. 'A penny a beast, and a penny the rider, and the dog goes free on account of I like dogs.' She held out her hand, palm up, and did not look at him. 'Ninety head?'
'Ninety.'
'It's ninety-two,' she said. 'You've two strays off the common in with them, I know their colour. But I'll take ninety, because you'll argue, and I've a kettle on.'

Wren sat Thistle at the back of the herd with her hands on the reins and her left arm held quiet against her body, and watched Ash count coins into the old woman's palm. He did it slowly and made a business of it, hamming it up, dropping one and catching it, and Mother Agate watched him do it with the flat patience of a woman who had watched drovers be charming for fifty years and had never once been moved.
'That's the beasts,' she said, and closed her hand on the coins, and then she looked past Ash, down the herd, to Wren. 'And the rider.'

Wren's purse was in the pocket of her jumper, and in the purse was a broken button and her grandfather's watch chain, folded small. Four pounds had gone to Thistle and five shillings was gone into Drake's Bottom, into Reuben's hand for the shoeing and a bag of oats and a strip of leather for the mare's nosebag, and she had counted the last of it out on his bench while he watched, and there was nothing left but the chain, and the chain would not buy a crossing.
She had known the toll was coming. She had known it since Ash said the bridge was at Haldon, and she had done her sums on the road and got the same answer every time, which was none.
'She's with me,' Ash said.

'She's a rider,' said Mother Agate. 'A rider's a penny, and I've took a penny off every rider that's crossed this bridge since I was forty and my husband before me, and I'll not stop now for the look of her.'
'I'll pay it.'
'You'll not.' Mother Agate shifted on the stool and set both hands on the stick. 'You paid for your beasts and that's your business. This is hers.'

Wren got down. Her legs had gone stiff in the cold of the afternoon and she came off the mare badly, catching herself with her right hand on the saddle and holding the left arm out from her side, and she felt the old woman's eyes go over the bandage from wrist to elbow, and the melted sleeve, and the way she stood. She got the purse out and opened it and held it open, so the old woman could see it: a button with the shank snapped off, and a length of watch chain gone the colour of old tea.
'That's all of it,' Wren said. 'I sold the watch at Fallow Cross. The chain's not silver. It's brass, and it's not worth a penny to anyone but me.'
Mother Agate looked in the purse a while. Then she looked at Wren's face, and at the case on the mare's back, and at the scorch mark on the leather of the case where the strap had burned.
'Surveyor?' she said.
'Apprentice.'
'Where bound?'
'Carrow.'
'That's a long way to walk for a penny,' said Mother Agate. 'What's in the case?'
Wren did not answer. The river went under the bridge, and one of the cattle lowed, and Thistle put her head down and pulled at the grass at the end of the parapet until Ash took her reins.
'Well,' Mother Agate said. 'A penny's a penny, and I'll have it off you one way or the other, girl, so you'd best find me something I want.'

Wren stood with the purse open in her hand. She thought about the button, which was nothing. She thought about the letter folded inside her jumper, which was not a thing you could hand to a woman on a bridge. She thought about the case, and the seal in the case, and knew that if she put it down on the parapet she might as well hand it to the Warden's men and save them the ride.

Then she put her right hand into the inside pocket of the jumper, under the letter, where the small hard shape had sat against her ribs for five days and every day before that since she was nine years old.

The compass was brass, and the lid of it was scratched all over from a life in pockets, and the glass over the needle was clouded at one edge where her grandmother had chipped it against a gatepost in a year Wren could not remember. Her grandfather had carried it on the levels at Linmouth for forty years and given it to his wife when he stopped, and his wife had given it to Wren on the day she was apprenticed, and had told her that a surveyor's whole trade was knowing which way was north when nobody could agree, and that the compass would tell her, and that she should never lend it to a man.

She had used it every day of her six years. The needle had a tremor in it now, a quarter of a point east of true, and she had learned to allow for the tremor the way she allowed for the run of a stream or the lie of a hedge, and she could read it faster than she could read a page.
She put it in Mother Agate's palm.
The old woman closed her fingers on it and held it up and turned it in the last of the light, and thumbed the lid open, and the needle swung and settled and trembled a quarter of a point east.
'Brass,' she said.
'Yes.'
'Good brass.'
'It was my grandmother's.'

Mother Agate shut the lid with her thumb and put the compass into the pocket of the coat gone the colour of the road, and it went down into that pocket and out of the world, and Wren felt the shape of it go from under her ribs where it had been for thirteen years.

'Then she'll not mind,' said Mother Agate, 'since she's dead and I'm not, and I've a kettle on.' She lifted the stick off her knees and pointed it at the bridge. 'Cross, then. And keep them off the parapet, Penrose, the last lot pushed a heifer over and I had to get her out of the shallows with a rope.'

Ash took Thistle's reins and led her onto the bridge, and Wren walked at the mare's head with her hand on the halter, and the herd came after them in a long brown shuffling line, hooves loud on the stone, and the dog working the tail of them along. The river ran under the arches, brown and quick, and Wren looked down at it once and then away, because there was nothing in it for her.

On the far side the road climbed away between the thorns. Ash swung up onto his horse and waited for her to mount, and she got her foot in the stirrup and her weight up over the saddle with her burned arm held clear, and Thistle shifted under her and settled, and they went on up the road, and behind them Mother Agate sat down on her stool again with her stick across her knees and waited for the next of them.

scenes.title: The beech wood

beats: In a beech wood two hired men try to drag Wren off her horse and take the survey case.
Ash fights them off with his drover’s stick; one has a knife.
The men run; Wren binds Ash’s wound.

paragraphs: The road went up out of the thorn hedges and into the beech wood, and under the trees the light went green and the air went cold.

Wren rode with her left arm held clear of her body as she had held it since the bridge, and Thistle walked with her head low, and behind them the herd made the low complaining noise cattle make on a road they do not know. The beeches were just coming into leaf, the new leaves thin and pale as if the light went through them, and the trunks stood up grey and smooth, and the ground under them was bare and brown with last year's mast.

Ash rode ahead of her, half turned in the saddle, talking. He had been talking since the bridge. He was telling her about a bull he had once walked from Harrowgate to Fallow Cross that had learned to open gates, and how he had had to tie every gate on the road behind him with a bit of string, and how the string had cost him more than the bull.

'And the worst of it,' he said, 'is that a beast like that learns the trick off you and then every other beast in the bunch wants the trick too, so you've ninety head of cattle all trying to lift a gate latch with their noses, and there's not an honest man on the road will believe you. They think you've left the gates open.'
Wren said, 'How far to the top of the wood?'

'Another mile. Then the open ground above the valley. Then Drake's Bottom tomorrow night, and Reuben will look at that mare of yours and tell me I've sold you a lame one, which I haven't.' He looked back at her. 'You're grey. When did you last eat?'
'This morning.'
'That's not what I asked.'

The wood narrowed where the old road cut through it, the bank rising steep on the left with the moss on it and the roots showing through, and the light coming down in long green stripes across the pale dust of the road. Wren heard the men before she saw them, which she would think about later — a shift of weight on the bank, a stone moved.
Two men came down the bank on her left, fast, out of the moss and the roots, and they were on her before Thistle had time to shy.

One got the reins near the bit and hauled the mare's head round, and she went back on her haunches and Wren came forward over the saddle horn and caught the case strap with her burned arm and the pain went up her shoulder white and hot. The other man had her by the leg and then by the waist, and he pulled, and she went off the horse sideways, and the ground came up and hit her shoulder and her arm and the world went red at the edges.

She kept hold of the case. She had her right arm through the strap and she lay on the case in the road dust with the man over her, and he had his hands on the strap and was pulling it up over her head, and his breath smelled of onions and he was saying, 'Let go of it, let go of it,' not loud, not angry, the way you would say it to a dog.
Then Ash was there.

He came off his horse in one movement and he had the stick with the knot in it and he brought it down across the man's shoulders and the man went down on his hands in the dust. The first man let go of the reins and came round the horse's head and Ash turned the stick and caught him across the wrist and the man swore and pulled back, and Thistle shied off down the road a little way and stood with her reins down, shaking.
'Get off her,' Ash said. 'Get off her and go on down the road and I'll not break your heads.'

The man on the ground got his feet under him and came up with a knife, a short one, a skinning knife, and he came at Ash low and quick, and Ash got the stick up and the knife went along the stick and the man's weight came in under it, and they went into the bank together, the two of them, and the knife went across Ash's face, from the eye down, left cheek, and the blood came at once and went down into the collar of his coat.

Wren was up on one knee in the road with the case held against her chest. She saw the blood and she saw Ash's face change, not to fear, to something else, something set, and he got the man's knife arm with his left hand and bent it back over his knee, and the man made a noise and dropped the knife, and Ash hit him once with the knot end of the stick, in the side of the head, and the man went down in the moss and did not get up.

The first man was already running. He went down the bank and through the trunks, and the light took him in stripes and then he was gone, and they heard him crashing down through the wood towards the river for a long while after.

The one in the moss got up on his hands and knees, and Ash stood over him with the stick and said nothing at all. The man got up and looked at Ash once, at his face, and then he went after the other one, holding his arm against his chest, and the wood took him too.
Ash stood in the road and put his hand up to his cheek and brought it away red.
'Ah,' he said.

Wren got the case off her shoulder and set it in the dust and got the purse out of her jumper. She had the watch chain in it and the broken button and nothing else. She put the purse down and got up and went to Thistle and took the nosebag off the saddle where it hung and tipped the oats out into the road, and then she went back to Ash with the nosebag in her hand.
'Sit down,' she said.
'I'm all right.'
'Sit down on the bank. You're bleeding into your coat.'

He sat. He sat down on the mossy bank with the stick across his knees and his hand up at his face, and she pulled the neck of his jumper down and got at the wound. It was long, from under his left eye down the cheek to the jaw, and the flap of the skin was open, and it was filling up as she watched. Behind her the cattle had stopped and stood in the road with their heads up, and further off she could hear Tom's voice and the dog working them.
She took the nosebag and wiped the blood off Ash's face with the cloth of it, and he winced and said, 'That's my breakfast bag.'
'It's a bag,' she said. 'Hold still.'

She thought about the linen. She had clean linen on her own arm, tied off at the elbow, and she could not spare it, and she did not have anything else except the coat on the saddle and the shirt she stood in, and the shirt was not clean. She looked at the two men's road, and there was nothing on it. Then she pulled the jumper up over her head, one-armed, careful with the burned arm, and the letter fell out into the moss and she picked it up and put it inside the case and closed the case, and then she took the jumper and got the hem of it and tore a strip off, which took both hands and her teeth and a long moment, and the wool gave at last with a sound like a cough.
'That's a good jumper,' Ash said.
'It's got a hole in the sleeve already.'

She folded the strip into a pad and put it along the wound and pressed, and he put his own hand over hers on the pad and pressed too, and they sat like that in the green light with the cattle lowing behind them. His hand was hot and his fingers were shaking, and she could feel it, and she did not say anything about it.
After a while she took the rest of the strip and bound it round his head, over the pad, under his ear and up over the crown and back, twice, and tied it off above his ear.
'Can you feel your teeth on that side?'
He worked his jaw. 'Aye.'
'Then it's not through the muscle. It'll knit. You'll have a scar like a duelling man.'
'I've never duelled in my life.'
'You have now.'

He laughed, and then stopped laughing, and put his fingers up to the bandage and touched it. His hand was still not steady. He looked down the road the way the men had gone, and then up the road, the way they had been going, and he was quiet for a moment.
'They weren't after the cattle,' he said.
'No.'
'They knew which of the ninety to come at.'

Wren put the jumper back on. It went over her head and down and the torn hem hung loose, and the letter was in the case and the case was at her feet in the road dust, and she looked at it and then she picked it up and put the strap over her shoulder.
'We should go on,' she said. 'They'll be back with more, or they'll be waiting at the top of the wood where it's open.'
Ash got up off the bank. He stood for a moment with his hand on the stick, and then he went to his horse, which had stood in the road all this while with its head down, and he gathered the reins.
'You'll want your mare,' he said. 'She went down the road a piece.'

Wren walked down the road and took up Thistle's reins and led her back. The mare's eye rolled white at Ash's bandage and then she settled. Wren got her foot in the stirrup and her weight up over the saddle with the burned arm held clear, and Ash swung up onto his horse, and the cattle started moving again behind them, the dog coming up the wood with them, and the two of them rode on up through the beeches towards the light at the top of the wood.

scenes.title: Hobb's Farm

beats: Wren's horse puts a foot in a rabbit hole on the moor.
They stop at Hobb's Farm; the farmer's wife says the injury needs weeks.
They go on.

paragraphs: They came out of the top of the wood into open moor, and the light was so wide after the green dark that Wren had to narrow her eyes against it. The road ran on over the tops in a long grey line, and the cattle spread out across it, and the dog ran behind them with its tongue out. Ash rode with his good side to her, the bandage white round his head, and neither of them said much. His hand on the reins was steadier than it had been. Hers was not.
They had gone two miles or a little more when Thistle put her near forefoot in a rabbit hole.

It was nothing, at the walk. The mare dropped into it and came out of it, and Wren felt the stumble go up through the saddle, and she gathered the reins and sat back and the mare went on three or four strides and then began to nod. Not the easy nod of a horse that has walked all day. A short, hard nod, down and up, down and up, in time with the off forefoot, and the ear on that side went back.
Wren pulled up. She sat a moment, and then she swung down, careful with the burned arm, and ran her hand down the leg.
The mare's off fore was hot at the coronet, and when Wren pressed the sole with her thumb the mare flinched and took the foot away and set it down again quickly, holding it.
'Rabbit hole,' Ash said. He had come back and sat his horse above her, looking down. 'I saw her go into it. It's the sole, or it's the foot.'
'It's the foot,' Wren said. She had her hand on the leg above the fetlock. It was hot there too.
Ash got down. He took the foot up himself, and the mare let him, and he turned it and looked at the sole and pressed it with his thumb the way Wren had, and the mare took it away from him too.
'Bruised,' he said. 'Deep. Maybe a bit of the hole in it, maybe a stone. She'll not carry you far on that.'
'She'll carry me to the top of the next rise.'

'She might. And then she'll go properly lame and you'll have a lame horse and a long walk and no horse at all.' He let the foot down and stood, and looked along the road ahead, and then past it, off to the left where the moor fell away towards a fold of green with a roof in it. 'There's Hobb's. Half a mile down the slack. He'll know what to do with her, or his wife will.'

Wren looked at the farm. It was a low place, long and grey, with a byre at one end and a stack of peat against the gable. Smoke went up straight from the chimney. It was the first chimney smoke she had seen since the ferry, and something in her chest turned over at the sight of it, and she did not look at the reason for that.
'We've the herd,' she said.
'Tom's got the herd. Tom's had the herd since Haldon. We'll catch them up at the nighting place on the top, and if we don't, they'll be there in the morning and so will we.'

She stood a moment with her hand on the mare's neck. The saddle and the case were on the mare's back, and the case on its strap over her own shoulder, and the letter inside the case, and everything she had left in the world was in the two of them.

'Come on,' Ash said. He took his horse's reins and led it off the road and down the slack, and Wren took Thistle's reins and followed, and the mare hopped and nodded and came on three legs and a half all the way down to the farm.

The farmer's wife was in the yard with a pail, a short woman with grey hair screwed back and forearms like a man's. She looked at the two of them, and at the bandage round Ash's head, and at the horse, and she set the pail down.
'That's a lame horse,' she said.
'She put her foot in a hole on the top,' Wren said. 'It's the off fore. It's hot at the coronet.'
'Bring her in.'

The byre was dark and warm and smelled of cattle and peat smoke. The woman took the foot up and did what Ash had done, and pressed it, and looked at the sole a long time with her thumb on it, and then she set the foot down and wiped her hands on her apron and looked at Wren.
'Bruise under the sole, and a bit of the hole gone into it. She wants a poultice and a fortnight in a box, and then a week of walking, and then you can put a saddle on her and see.'
'A fortnight,' Wren said.

'Weeks,' the woman said. 'Not days. If you take her out of here tomorrow she'll go lame for good and you'll have nothing but a field ornament with a black stripe down her.' She looked at Wren's arm, at the clean linen tied off at the elbow, and at the way Wren was holding it. 'And you've got a hurt of your own there, by the look of you. You're not long off a burn.'
'It's knitting.'

'They all knit, till they don't.' The woman picked up her pail again. 'You can leave her here. I'll poultice her and feed her and she'll be sound by the back end of the month, and you can send for her or come back for her. I've no use for a lame horse and I'll not sell her on you, if that's what you're chewing on. I'll want paying for the feed.'

Wren stood in the byre with her hand on the mare's shoulder. Thistle had her head down, the way she stood in the field at Fallow Cross, one hip cocked, unbothered, and she was warm under Wren's hand and she was the only thing Wren had bought with her own money in her life.
'How much?' Wren said.
'Two shillings the fortnight, and I'll take it when you come back for her, or I'll take it now if you've got it.'
Wren had a broken button and her grandfather's chain.
'I'll bring it when I come,' she said. 'I'll come back for her. My name's Wren Hollis, and I'm bound for Carrow, and I'll come back.'

The woman looked at her a moment longer than was comfortable. 'They all say that,' she said. 'Well. Leave the tack on the peg and go on. There's a grey in the small field that'll carry you if your man wants to sell him.'
'He's not my man,' Wren said.
The woman went out with her pail.

Wren took the saddle off herself, and the case off the saddle, and hung the saddle and the bridle on the peg. She rubbed the mare down with a wisp of straw, working round the sore foot, and the mare stood and let her, and when Wren put her hand flat on the black stripe down the spine the mare turned her head round and looked at her with the half-lidded dark eye and then put her head back down and pulled at the hay in the rack. That was all. She did not care. She was a horse who took no particular interest in strangers, and Wren had had her six days.
Wren put her forehead against the mare's neck for a moment and then took her hand away and went out.

Ash was in the yard with the farmer, a thin man in a coat the colour of the byre wall, and there was a grey gelding on a halter by the gate, a tall plain horse with a white nose and a ribby look to him. The farmer named a price. Ash looked at the horse's legs and his feet and his eye, and then he counted out coins into the man's hand, and the man went off with them into the house.
'He's called Cinder,' Ash said. 'He's no beauty and he's got a mouth on him, but he's sound and he'll go all day. He's the spare. He's been on a leading rein since Haldon and he's fresh.'
'Ash —'
'You'll not walk to Carrow on that arm,' he said. 'And I'll not lead you on a rope like a calf all the way to Harrowgate. Take him.'
She looked at the grey. He looked back at her, unimpressed.
'When the mare's sound I'll sell him back or keep him and pay you,' she said.
'You'll do neither,' Ash said. 'He's mine. I'm lending him. That's a different thing and you know it.'

She did know it. She took the halter and led Cinder out of the yard, and got her foot in the stirrup, and the gelding stood while she got up, which was more than Thistle had done the first time, and Ash got up on his own horse beside her, and they rode out of the yard onto the track and back up onto the road, and the farm went down behind them into the fold of green with the smoke going up straight, and Wren did not look back at it, because there was nothing to be done about looking back, and there was a long way still to go.

scenes.title: The Drover's Rest

beats: They bring the cattle into Harrowgate and stable the horses at the Drover’s Rest.
Sela Marr, the landlady, asks a hundred questions.
Wren takes a small room under the roof.

paragraphs: Harrowgate came up out of the flat country all at once, the way a town does when the road has been climbing towards it for two days and the walls are the colour of the dust you have been eating.

They brought the cattle in through the north gate at the tail end of the afternoon, and the whole road in front of them filled with noise. Drovers ahead of them, drovers behind. A flock of geese going the other way, and a woman with a barrow of eels shouting over the top of it. The herd wanted to string out and look at everything, and Tom and the dog worked them along the outside of the market wall where the pens began, and Ash rode up front with his stick across his lap and his bandage a dirty grey now, and Wren rode Cinder at the tail with the case on her shoulder and her reins loose the way the grey liked them.

The smell was the first thing. Smoke and dung and wet stone and bread. After eight days of moor and wood and the inside of her own head, the smell of a place where people lived came at her so hard she had to sit up straighter on the horse.
They put the herd in the pens by the cattle market, and Tom went off to find his brother, and Ash walked the horses the short way down the lane to the Drover's Rest.

It was a long stone building with a slate roof and a lamp already lit in the doorway though it was not dark yet, and it stood side-on to the market so you could hear the lowing through the wall. A girl came out and took the horses, and Ash asked after a stall and a box, and there was a deal done about hay and about Cinder's feed, and Wren stood in the yard with the case on her shoulder and watched the light going orange along the top of the wall.
The door of the inn opened onto a room with a fire in it and benches and a great many people.
Sela Marr came out from behind the bar with a cloth over her shoulder and looked Wren up and down in one go, the case, the bandage, the burnt sleeve, and smiled with her whole face.
'Well,' she said. 'You'll be the first dry thing that's come through that door all day, and I'll take it. Sit. Sit down before you fall down. What's your name?'
'Wren Hollis.'

'Hollis. Hollis.' Sela wiped the table with the cloth, though the table was clean. 'I know Hollises. Not that kind of Hollis, I shouldn't think, they're down by the water and there's a lot of them. Are you eating? You're eating. You look like a scarecrow that's been rained on. Where've you come from?'
'Linmouth.'
'Linmouth!' Sela set down two bowls without being asked. 'That's a long walk.'
'I had a horse.'
'And the arm?'
'Burned it.'
'On what?'
'A lamp.'
Sela's eyes went to the case, sitting on the bench beside Wren with its strap still over her shoulder. Wren made herself not move it.
'And your man there with his face bound up like a pudding. He's a drover, is he? He has the look.'
'He brought the cattle up.'
'Penrose. I know him, he's been in here before, he'll be in here again. He'll be telling the girls about the time the bull opened the gate. Are you his?'
'No.'
'Good,' Sela said. 'Not that he's a bad one. He's a bad one. Are you wool?'

Wren had the lie ready, and she had had it ready since Fallow Cross, and it was a lie she could have said in her sleep, because she had spent two days making it fit. 'I'm a wool buyer,' she said. 'Out of Linmouth. There's a man there sends me up to look at the fleeces at the Thursday market and see what the fell flocks are bringing.'
'In July?'
'He buys early.'
Sela nodded slowly, the way a person nods at a thing they have decided to believe for now. 'And you carry a case for wool.'
'My samples. And my books.'
