'Books,' Sela said, with great satisfaction, as though Wren had told her something much more interesting than she had. 'There's a girl under the roof who reads. She's the one to ask if you want the news of the town. Now. Soup, bread, a bed, or you'll be no use to any man's fleeces.'

She brought the soup herself, and the bread, and a jug of small beer, and she asked after the road, and the state of the bridge at Haldon, and whether the toll-keeper was still alive, and when Wren said she was, Sela said that woman will bury us all and charge us for the digging.

Ash came in with the coat off and the bandage rewound, and sat down on the other side of the table with his good side to the room, and ate like a man who had been counting cattle for a week. Sela put a bowl in front of him without being asked and said, 'And what happened to your face, Ash Penrose?'
'Fell on a gate,' Ash said.
'You fell on a gate.'
'In the dark.'
'I've seen a gate or two,' Sela said, 'and I've never seen one with a knife in it.'

Ash put bread in his mouth and chewed, and Sela, seeing she would get nothing, went off to the next table to get nothing out of the men there, and they heard her laughing at something before she reached them.
'She'll have your name in the town by morning,' Ash said, quietly, not looking at Wren.
'I know.'
'Wool,' he said.
'It's the nearest true thing,' Wren said. 'There's wool in it. There's paper in it and the paper's about land and the land has sheep on it, some of it. It'll hold.'
'It'll hold,' Ash agreed. 'If she asks you the price of a fleece you'd better know it.'
'I know the price of a fleece.'

'Of course you do.' He tore the bread in half. 'You know the price of everything. That's what worries me about you.' He ate, and then he said, 'I'll be off first light with Tom. There's a man at the assay office wants the herd counted in before the market opens, and it'll take the morning. You'll be all right here?'
'I'll be all right here.'
'I'll come back for you at noon.'
'Ash.'

'At noon,' he said, and that was the end of it, and he went out to see to his horse, and Wren sat with the last of the beer and the case on the bench beside her and the room going on all round her, and nobody in it looked at her twice.

Sela showed her up herself, up two flights, the stair turning tighter at the top, and opened a door into a room under the roof with one small window and a bed with a straw tick and a chest and a nail on the wall.

'It's small,' Sela said, 'but the roof's sound and there's no one over you, and the window looks at the wall which is the best view in Harrowgate for sleeping. Two shillings the week, paid when you can.'
Wren paid her the week out of what Ash had refused to take back, and Sela said goodnight and lingered in the doorway a moment, looking at the room, at the case, at Wren.
'The Assize sits in three weeks,' Sela said. 'There's a fair bit of coming and going for it. Wool men, mostly.'
'Mostly,' Wren said.
Sela went down, and her feet went a long way down, and the door at the bottom of the stairs opened and shut.

Wren put the case on the chest and stood a long time at the little window with her hand flat on the lid. Below her the market wall was grey and the lamps were being lit along the lane, one by one, on down the hill towards the sound of the river somewhere past the roofs. The town was between her and Carrow. Nothing else was.

scenes.title: The Assay Office

beats: Wren asks at the Assay Office how a survey claim is registered.
A sneering clerk tells her it must be laid before the Carrow Assize in person, by midsummer.
She counts the days left.

paragraphs: Wren was awake before the bell rang for the market, lying on the straw tick with the case against her hip and the room grey around her. Her arm had leaked through the bandage in the night and stuck to the sheet, and she worked it free slowly, biting down on nothing. The smell was goose grease and clean linen, at least, and not the other thing. She sat on the edge of the bed and unwound the bandage to look. The blisters had gone down a little at the wrist. The little red flowers were still there, stamped into her skin above them, and she looked at those the way she looked at a bad total in a field book until she had looked long enough, and then she wound the linen back on, one-handed, using her teeth at the end.

She dressed and went down. The inn was already loud. Drovers and carters filled the long room, and Sela was moving among them with a jug in each hand, and the fire had been built up, and the whole place smelled of porridge and wet wool. Wren ate standing at the end of the bench, watching the door for Ash and not seeing him, and when Sela came past she said, 'The assay office. Where is it?'
'Up the lane past the market cross, the stone front with the steps. You'll see the queue.' Sela looked at the case on Wren's shoulder. 'Wool men don't queue there.'
'I'll queue,' Wren said, and went out.

Harrowgate in the morning was a different town from the one she had walked into at dusk. The lane up from the inn was packed to the walls with stalls going up, trestles and boards and hurdles, and men carrying geese upside down, and a woman with a barrow of eels shouting the price of eels at everyone who passed. The market wall ran grey along the top of the street with the sky pale above it, and the smell was smoke and dung and wet stone and bread, all of it at once, and under it the river somewhere she still could not see. Wren kept the case strap across her chest and her burned arm inside her coat and went up the hill.

The Assay Office was a stone front with three steps and a door standing open, and inside, a counter, and behind the counter, a clerk writing at a ledger with his sleeve held back by a pin. There was no queue. There was a man in a good coat ahead of her, and he was done in a moment, and then Wren was at the counter with the case on it and her hand flat on the lid.
'I want to register a survey,' she said.
The clerk did not look up. 'Register what?'
'A survey. Of land. My master made it and it's finished and it wants putting on the record.'

The clerk finished his line, blotted it, and looked at her then, and looked at the case, and looked at her again, at the bandage coming out of her cuff, at the coat that had been a man's coat. He had a long pale face and the patience of a man who had been asked stupid questions all morning.
'You're not from here.'
'Linmouth.'
'And your master?'
'Edric Rone. Surveyor.'
The clerk's pen stopped. It was a small thing, but Wren had spent three years watching Edric read men's faces across a table, and she saw it. He knew the name. He wrote nothing down.
'Linmouth,' he said. 'Under whose grant?'
'I don't follow.'
'The land. Whose is it?'
'It's fell land above Carrow. It's in the Crown grant, some of it, and the rest—'

'Then it's not mine to register,' the clerk said. 'This is the assay office. We assay metal. We keep the town's weights, we stamp the plate, we take the fees on cattle counted in. Surveys of land go to the Assize.'
'I know that,' Wren said. 'I'm asking how.'

'You lay it before the Assize. In person. The surveyor or his sworn deputy stands up and lays the instrument and the field books and the seal before the court, and the court receives it, and it goes on the record, and then it's registered.' He said the words as though he had said them a hundred times, and he probably had. 'Not here. Not before a clerk at a counter.'
'Then I'll lay it before the Assize.'
'You'll lay it before the Carrow Assize,' the clerk said. 'This is Harrowgate. The Assize sits at Carrow. It's a different town and a different court and it's forty miles from this door.'

She had known the number. She had known it since Oskar Venn stood on his punt and told her a hundred miles round by Harrowgate bridge, and she had been counting it down ever since, the way she counted cattle, the way she counted everything. But knowing a number and hearing it read out by a clerk with a pen in his hand were two different things.
'When does it sit?' she said.

'It sits at midsummer,' the clerk said, 'and rises when it's done, and if you've not laid your instrument before it rises you'll wait another year for the next, and the year after that if it pleases them. That's the law and I don't make it.' He dipped his pen. 'Midsummer's the twenty-first. You've nineteen days.'

Wren stood at the counter with her hand on the case and did the sum in her head, the way she did every sum, and did it again to be sure. Today was the ninth of the month. Nineteen days to Carrow, forty miles of road, and the Assize rising on the twenty-first, and after that nothing but waiting, and Warden Vey's men waiting with her, and the survey going soft in its case like fruit.
'And if a man wanted it registered in two names,' she said. 'His and mine. His being dead.'
The clerk's pen hovered. 'Dead when?'
'The day it was finished. The day before I left.'

'Then you'd swear to it,' the clerk said. 'You'd stand up and swear he made it and you carried it and it's true as he left it. They don't much like a dead man's survey laid by a living hand, but they'll take it if you swear.' He looked at her bandage again, and then at her face, and something in his own face went a little sour, as though he had decided she was not worth the trouble of being kind to. 'You'll want to be gone from here, then. Nineteen days is not many, and the road to Carrow is not a good road.'
'I know the road,' Wren said.
'Do you.'
'I'll know it better.'

She took the case off the counter and put the strap back over her shoulder, and the clerk had already gone back to his ledger, and she went down the three steps into the lane where the eel woman was still shouting the price of eels. The market wall stood grey over the rooftops and the sun was up over it, and somewhere south and east of that wall, past forty miles of road and a town called Carrow and a fell she had never seen, a court would sit on the twenty-first of the month whether she was there or not.
Nineteen days.
She turned back down the hill to find Ash, and to be standing in the yard of the Drover's Rest at noon.

scenes.title: Questions at the inn

beats: Gale arrives at the Drover’s Rest asking after a young woman from Linmouth with a leather case.
From the stairs Wren hears Sela tell him the only Linmouth girl here is a wool buyer.
Gale leaves; Wren does not sleep.

paragraphs: Wren spent the afternoon in the yard, because the yard was where Ash would come and because the room under the roof had begun to feel like a box with the lid on. She rubbed Cinder down with a wisp of straw, picked the dried mud out of his white nose, and moved her feet when he moved his, which he did whenever he thought she had stopped paying attention. The cattle market stank of dung and trodden grass. Beyond the wall, Harrowgate went on with its business: carts, geese, a bell somewhere, the eel woman still shouting, though the price had changed since morning.
By evening the market had thinned to straw and droppings and men rolling barrels. Ash did not come.

She ate in the taproom with her back to the wall and the case on the bench beside her under her hand. Sela brought her mutton and a baked apple and did not ask her anything for once, only looked at the empty chair opposite and said, ‘Your man not back?’
‘He’s not my man,’ Wren said.
‘That’s the way of it, mostly,’ Sela said, and went off to a table of carters who were singing something about a girl in Fallow Cross.

Wren took the stairs at full dark. Her room was under the roof, a bed and a stool and a jug, with a small window looking down into the market and along the lane to the north gate. She unwound the bandage and looked at the burn by candlelight. The blisters had gone down at the wrist, where the skin was beginning to look like skin again, but higher up the arm the red flowers of Edric’s shirt cuff still stood in the flesh, and the linen had stuck in the night and taken a little of the weeping with it. She cleaned it, greased it, wound it one-handed with her teeth on the end of the linen, and sat down on the stool with her back to the cold chimney breast, the case across her knees.
Nineteen days from this morning. Eighteen from tomorrow.

She did not know how long she had been sitting there when the knock came. Three taps, soft, unhurried, one and then two, the way a man knocks who has knocked at a great many doors and never once been in a hurry to get in.

Wren was on her feet before she knew it. The candle guttering, the case in both hands, the window, the door, the room with nowhere in it to be. Her heart was going like a hare’s and she made herself stand still and count her own breath the way she counted cattle, one and two and three, because counting was the one thing that had never yet failed her.
Below, the latch lifted. Sela’s voice came up the stairwell, warm and carrying, the way it carried to every corner of the house.
‘Well, now. You’ll be the last one through that door tonight and I’ll take you, but you’ll have to have something. What’ll it be?’

A man’s voice, low, courteous, pitched so that the room had to lean towards it. ‘Nothing for me. I’m looking for someone, as it happens, and I’d rather not trouble you long. A young woman. Came up from Linmouth, I think, in the last day or two. Reddish hair. She’d have a leather case with her, brass corners, a surveyor’s sort of case. You’d remember it.’
Wren put her hand flat on the wall. The plaster was cold and gritty under her palm and she kept it there, kept it still, and listened.
A pause. She could see Sela in her mind’s eye, cloth over the shoulder, taking the man in from boots to hat, deciding what he was worth.
‘Linmouth,’ Sela said, drawing it out. ‘We get them from everywhere, love. Drovers, carters, wool men, all sorts, and half of them can’t remember where they started from. Reddish hair, you say?’
‘Reddish. Small. She’d be carrying it strapped on her, I think. She wouldn’t let it out of her sight.’
‘That sounds like a young woman with something worth keeping,’ Sela said. ‘Are you sure you won’t have a drop? Cold night for the time of year.’
‘You’re kind. The young woman.’

‘Well,’ Sela said, and Wren heard the cloth come off the shoulder and go over the table, one slow wipe and then another, the sound of a woman taking her time because the time was hers to take. ‘The only Linmouth girl under this roof came in with the herd yesterday and she’s a wool buyer out of Linmouth, which is not the same as a girl from Linmouth, if you follow me, and she’s up in her bed this hour with her samples and her books, and I don’t wake paying guests to show them to strangers. If you’re after a fleece you’ll do better at the market in the morning. Thursday. There’s wool coming in from all over.’
‘A wool buyer,’ the man said. ‘With a surveyor’s case.’

‘I didn’t say surveyor. You said surveyor. I said she has a case, like every soul that travels with anything at all. The drovers have cases. The tinkers have cases. I’ve a case of my own under the stairs with the good spoons in it.’ Another wipe of the cloth. ‘Is there someone in this town you’re missing, love? Because I know most of them, and I’ll tell you straight if I do.’

A silence then, and Wren stood with her hand on the wall and her ears stretched down the stairwell, and the silence went on long enough that she started counting again, one and two and three and four, and by seven she had begun to think he had gone, and by nine she knew he had not.
‘No,’ the man said at last. ‘No, I don’t believe there is. You’ve been very good. I’ll wish you goodnight.’
‘Goodnight to you,’ Sela said. ‘And if you change your mind about that drop, it’ll be here in the morning and the morning after, and I don’t water it, whatever they tell you about this town.’

The door opened and shut. Wren stayed where she was, hand on the wall, and heard Sela go on working the room below, her voice moving from table to table, and after a while the carters started up their song again about the girl in Fallow Cross, and a stool scraped, and someone laughed.
She went to the window.

The lane ran down from the north gate along the market wall, and a lamp burned in the doorway of the Drover’s Rest, throwing a yellow bar across the cobbles. A man walked out of that bar of light into the dark. Grey coat, hat in his hand, his boots making no particular sound on the stones. He did not look up at the windows. He walked down the lane unhurried, past the pen where the cattle had stood, and where the lane met the wider street he stopped and stood a moment under the corner lamp, and then he went on, south, towards the river.

Wren watched until the grey went out of him and there was only dark. Then she sat down on the edge of the bed with the case against her ribs and her burned arm cradled over it, and she did not undress, and she did not lie down.

The candle went out on its own. The market bell rang the hours and she counted them, and at some point in the small hours Cinder stamped once in his box below and she heard it through the floor, and after that there was nothing but the town breathing, and the window going from black to grey, and her own hands on the case, and the eighteen days going down to seventeen.

scenes.title: Thursday market

beats: Ash sells his cattle at the Thursday market for a good price.
Wren wanders the stalls.
They eat hot pies on the cathedral steps.

paragraphs: By full light the lane below the window had filled with beasts and men, and the noise came up through the floorboards like water rising. Wren had heard the market bell at six and again at seven, and at eight she stood at the glass with the case strapped under her coat and watched the pens fill. Sheep first, then cattle, then the lowing and the shouting, and a woman below her window calling the price of eels, and over all of it the smell of smoke and dung and wet stone and bread.
She went down at nine, because sitting still had begun to feel like waiting to be found. Sela had a bowl of porridge on the bar before Wren had her second foot off the stair.
‘You’ll want that in you,’ Sela said. ‘Thursday. Every soul in the county is in the lane today and half of them want feeding.’
Wren ate standing, watching the door. She had counted the hours to nothing and they had come to nothing.

‘Your drover came in at first light,’ Sela said, wiping the bar. ‘Went up to the pen with the rest of them. Herd counted in before the bell, which is more than some managed. You’ll find him up the market with the beasts, and if you want my advice you’ll take your own purse, because he’ll have his out and he’ll lose it in the first hour, they always do.’

Wren went out into the lane. The pens along the market wall ran the whole length of it, and the beasts in them were packed shoulder to shoulder, and the men between the pens were packed the same. She kept her burned arm inside her coat and her good hand on the strap across her chest and went up the hill with the crowd, past a goose carried upside down under a man’s arm, past a woman with a barrow of eels shouting the price of eels, past two children with a basket of eggs and no intention of selling them where anyone could see.

She found Ash at the far pen with his boot on the rail, counting. He had his hat back and his coat on and the bandage round his head, and the wound under it had gone from grey to a kind of yellow at the edges that she did not like. He did not turn his head to look at her. He turned his whole body.

‘Ninety-two,’ he said. ‘Same as left Fallow Cross. I’ve sold ninety of them and kept the two strays, and I’ve had a price off the wool man and a better price off the butcher, and I’ve taken the butcher’s, which I’ll hear about from Tom until the day I die.’ He tapped the rail. ‘Nineteen pound eleven and six. Count it yourself if you don’t believe me, the money’s in the coat.’
‘I believe you,’ Wren said.
‘Then say something about it. It’s a good price. A very good price. I’ve had worse on a Tuesday and called it a living.’
‘It’s a good price,’ she said.
He looked at her properly then, and whatever was in his face went behind the bandage and stayed there. ‘You didn’t sleep,’ he said.

‘There was a man at the door last night. Sela sent him off. He went south towards the river and he didn’t look up at the windows, and I watched him go and he was grey all over, coat and all, and he had no mud on him and it’s been dry nine days.’
Ash was quiet a moment. In the pen behind him a beast shifted its weight and the whole row of them shifted with it, like one animal thinking. ‘Gale,’ he said.
‘It fits him.’

‘Then we don’t stand in the middle of a street talking about it.’ He took his boot off the rail. ‘Come on. I’ve a morning’s work done and no work till noon, and I’ve not eaten since the nighting place, and there’s a pie man up by the cross who owes me a favour from the year before last, which he’ll deny, and then I’ll pay him like a stranger and he’ll be pleased with himself all day.’

They went down and then up again, against the crowd this time, and the crowd did not mind because it was going both ways at once. The stalls ran back from the market cross in three rows, and the noise in them was the noise of a town that had decided for one day to be loud. Wren kept her hand on the case and let Ash go ahead of her where the men were thickest, and he made a way the way a big man makes a way, without seeming to notice he was doing it.

She stopped at a stall that sold thread and pins and buttons, and looked at the buttons, and bought nothing. She stopped at a stall where a man sold knives off a board and watched him sharpen one and put it back. She stopped where an old woman sold bread and did not buy bread, because she had money and did not want to spend it, which was a new and strange feeling and she turned it over while she walked.

At the third row, past the cheese, there was a glass-maker. He had a trestle and a cloth and on the cloth the whole trade laid out small: green bottles, a red bird with a chipped beak, buttons, a string of beads the colour of ditchwater, and in a shallow dish, loose, a dozen beads of blue glass the size of a pea, each one with a white thread through it.
Wren stood in front of the dish.
‘Two coppers the lot,’ the man said. ‘Or a penny each and I’ll not be hurried about it.’

She picked one up. It was warm from the sun, and the blue went right through it, and when she held it against the light it went the colour of the sky over the moor at Fallow Cross, and she thought of a girl barefoot in a punt with her hand out for the bread and her face doing the arithmetic of a promise.
‘One,’ she said. ‘This one.’

She paid the penny and put the bead in the pocket of her jumper, in the corner where the hem had torn away, and she pulled the loose thread across it so it could not get out, and then she walked on and found Ash at the pie man’s with two pies already in his hands.
‘You’ve bought something,’ he said.
‘Yes.’
‘What?’
‘A bead.’
He looked at her. ‘For the case?’
‘For a girl on the ferry at the Linn. I said I’d bring her one from Harrowgate market and I’ve been two days in Harrowgate and not done it, and now I’ve done it, and it’s one thing off the list.’
He handed her a pie. ‘You keep a list?’
‘I keep accounts,’ Wren said. ‘It’s the same thing with worse handwriting.’

They ate the pies walking, and the pies were hot and the fat ran down and the meat in them was good, and at the top of the hill the cathedral stood with its steps going up in a wide sweep, worn hollow in the middle of every one of them, and the whole width of the steps was full of people sitting and eating and arguing and sleeping off the morning. Ash found a place at the end of a step in the sun and sat down with his back against the wall and his legs out, and Wren sat beside him with the case on her lap.

For a while neither of them said anything. Below them the market went on, the eel woman still going, the geese still upside down, and a man with a cart of turnips arguing with a man with a cart of nothing, and the bells of the cathedral ringing the half hour over all of it, and the stones warm through her trousers, and the sun on the bandage on her arm.
‘Nineteen days,’ Ash said, not looking at her. ‘Eighteen now, from this morning.’
‘Seventeen from tomorrow,’ Wren said.
‘And when you get to Carrow with it, what then? What does it look like, the thing you’re doing?’

Wren watched a child run up the steps and down again, twice, for no reason. ‘I go in with the case. I lay the instrument and the field books and the seal on the table in front of the Assize and I swear he made it and I carried it, and it’s true as he left it. And then it’s on the record, and it can’t be unwritten, and a man can’t swear his own survey over the top of it, and that’s all. That’s the whole of it.’
‘That’s all,’ Ash said.
‘That’s all.’

He finished his pie and wiped his hand on his coat, which was mended in several colours, and looked out over the market and counted something under his breath, the way he did, without moving his lips, and she knew he was counting the herd that was no longer there.
‘Well,’ he said. ‘There’s worse ways to spend a Thursday.’

scenes.title: Cousin Bryn

beats: Ash’s cousin Bryn Tally, a carter and farrier, comes to the Drover’s Rest to meet him.
Bryn teases Ash about his healing face and looks Wren over without warmth.
Bryn offers them places on her cart going west.

paragraphs: They came down off the steps in the middle of the afternoon, when the shadow of the cathedral had reached the far side of the market and the eel woman had finally sold out and gone home. Ash walked Cinder out of the inn yard and up the lane to the blacksmith at the top of the hill to have a shoe tightened, and Wren went with him as far as the market cross and then turned back, because the case was heavy and her arm had begun to ache under the bandage and there was nothing at the top of the hill but a smith and a man who wanted a shoe.

Back at the Drover's Rest the taproom was nearly empty. Two carters sat in the window with a jug between them, and Sela was wiping down the long table with the cloth she kept over her shoulder, moving the benches out and in as she went.
'Your man's not back,' Sela said.
'He's not my man.'

'He's not back, all the same.' She straightened up and looked at Wren, and her look was the same as it had been the first night, taking in the case and the arm and the coat. 'There's a woman been asking after him. Not for you, for him. Penrose. She's sat in the corner yonder an hour and drunk nothing but water, and I'll not have it said the Drover's Rest turns a paying customer out into the street, so if she's a friend of his you might go and say so.'

Wren looked where Sela's chin pointed. In the corner by the chimney, where the light was worst, a woman sat with her back to the wall and her hands flat on the table in front of her, and beside her bench there was a cart whip coiled and a leather apron folded over it, and she was watching the door and the room and Wren and the door again, in that order, without any hurry about it.
'That's Bryn Tally,' Sela said. 'Carter. Farrier. She'd shoe a horse and tell you what's wrong with you while she did it. Ash's cousin, if you believe either of them.'

The woman in the corner had already seen them talking. She did not wave. She picked up her cup of water, drank the last of it, and set it down again with the flat of her hand over the top of it, as if to say the water was done and so was the waiting.

Wren crossed the room with the case against her side. Up close the woman was wide through the shoulders and had a burn scar of her own across the back of one hand, old and white and shining like a glove that would not come off.
'You'll be the wool buyer,' Bryn said.
'I'm the wool buyer.'

'Sela says you're out of Linmouth and buying fleeces at the Thursday market, and Sela says a lot of things, and half of them are true.' She looked Wren up and down, the way a farrier looks at a leg, and did not trouble to make it friendly. 'You're small for it.'
'It's a small trade.'

'Mm.' Bryn moved the leather apron off the bench with one hand. 'Sit, then, wool buyer. He'll be a while. That blacksmith at the top of the hill hasn't had two words out of anybody since the frost and he'll take his time over a shoe.'
Wren sat. The bench was warm where the apron had been.

'You want to know how I know him,' Bryn said. 'I'll save you the asking. His mother was my father's sister, and when he was twenty and had nothing and nowhere, he came and slept in my father's loft over the shop for the better part of a year, and ate our bread, and taught my youngest to whistle through her teeth, which I have not forgiven him for. So when he sends word by a carter coming up from the south that he's in Harrowgate and wants me at the Drover's Rest, I come to the Drover's Rest. I don't come for the ale.'
'He sent word?'
'Tuesday. Carter called Fenn, coming up with hides.' Bryn's eyes went past Wren to the door and stayed there. 'Here he is, and there's the face.'

Ash came in from the lane with the light behind him, hat in his hand, and the taproom turned and looked at him the way taprooms do and then went back to its jug. The bandage was gone. The wound under his left eye had closed into a thin pink line, raised a little, running from the cheekbone down to the jaw, and the yellow that had been at its edges had gone, and the skin around it had browned in the sun so that the scar stood out pale against the brown. He had the look of a man who had been out in weather and was glad of a wall.
'Bryn,' he said.
'Ash.'
He crossed the room and she stood up and they held each other by the shoulders, once, hard, and then let go, and Bryn sat back down and looked at him across the table with her hands folded.
'Well,' she said. 'That's a duelling scar if ever I saw one. Did you win?'
'I'm standing.'
'You're standing and the other fellow isn't, or you're standing and the other fellow's standing somewhere else. Which is it?'
'Somewhere else,' Ash said. 'For now.'

'Mm.' She looked at the scar properly, the way she had looked at Wren, with no softness in it. 'Clean, at least. Whoever sewed it knew what they were doing, or whoever didn't sew it left it alone, which is sometimes the same thing. That'll be a line on you the rest of your life. You'll be able to tell any story you like about it and no one will be able to say different.'
'I've been telling them I fell on a gate.'
'You fell on a gate.' Bryn's mouth moved at one corner, not quite a smile. 'You fell on a gate and the gate had a knife.'

Ash pulled a bench out with his foot and sat down. Sela came over without being asked and put three cups and a jug on the table and went away again, and Ash poured for himself and for Bryn, and Bryn put her hand over the cup and shook her head, and he poured for Wren instead and she took it, because her arm hurt and the beer was small and there was nothing else to do with her hands.
'So,' Bryn said. 'You've sold the herd.'
'Sold ninety. Nineteen pound eleven and six. The butcher's price, and I took it, because the price was going down the hill faster than I could walk the beasts up it.'
'And the two strays?'
'Kept them.'
'Of course you kept them.' She turned her cup a quarter-turn on the table. 'And now you're going west.'
'Now I'm going west,' Ash said.

Bryn looked at Wren. It was not the look she had given her before, over the bench and the apron. It was slower and it went further, and it stopped on the case, which Wren had set on the floor between her feet with her heel against it.

'You're going west,' Bryn said, to Ash, without looking away from Wren, 'and the wool buyer's going with you, and the wool buyer's got a surveyor's case between her feet and a burned arm she keeps inside her coat, and I'm a carter, so I notice what's on the cart.'
Nobody said anything. One of the carters in the window laughed at something and the other one said he hadn't said that.

'I'm not asking,' Bryn said. 'I've been in this town thirty-four years and I know when a person's carrying something that isn't mine to know. I'll say the one thing and then I'll drink my water and go. I've a cart going west day after tomorrow, loads of salt fish and dyed cloth for Fallow Cross and the villages under the fell, and I've a man short because my brother's gone to his wife's people at Carrow and taken the strong arm of the family with him. Two places on the cart. It's slow, but it's covered, and the roads west are dry, and I've never lost a load.' She looked at Ash. 'You and the girl. You'd be off the road and under the canvas, and nobody looks under canvas at a carter, because carters smell of fish.'
Ash looked at Wren.

Wren thought about the forty miles, and the seventeen days, and the grey-coated man walking south down the lane with his hat in his hand and no mud on him, and the case between her feet with a dead man's seal in it, and the road out of Harrowgate going west with a carter's canvas over her head and the smell of salt fish in her nose the whole way.
'Which road west?' she said.
Bryn Tally turned and looked at her for a moment with her flat, unhurried eyes.
'You'd be on it by noon,' she said.

scenes.title: What Ash told

beats: Bryn asks why a wool buyer needs to get to Carrow so badly.
Wren finds out Ash has said too much, and is furious with him.
In the end she accepts Bryn as one of them.

paragraphs: Bryn Tally drank her water. She set the cup down with the flat of her hand over the top of it, the way a person does when they have finished with a thing, and she looked at Wren across the table, and the corner by the chimney was dark enough that Wren could not read her face at all.
'Now,' Bryn said. 'The wool buyer.'
Wren put her own cup down.

'Linmouth wool,' Bryn said. 'Fleeces at the Thursday market. Books and samples in a case with brass corners on it, and a burned arm you keep inside a man's coat in the middle of summer.' She turned her cup a quarter-turn. 'I'm not asking what's in the case. I said that. I'll hold to it. But I'll ask you the one thing, because I'm giving you a place on my cart and my cart goes where I say, and I've a right to know where I'm stopping.'
'Ask it,' Wren said.
'Why does a wool buyer need Carrow so badly?'

The room went on around them. Two carters by the window were arguing about a horse; Sela was at the far end with her cloth over her shoulder, working a bench of drovers. The light behind Ash was going long and yellow in the lane, and the shadow of the cathedral had come all the way across the market and laid itself over the cobbles by the inn door.

Wren looked at Bryn and thought about the lie, which was a good lie, which had held at Hobb's and at the ferry and at the assay office counter. It would hold here. It was the nearest true thing, and the nearest true thing will hold.

Then Ash moved beside her. He took his hat off the table and turned it over in his hands, and he did not look at her, and he did not look at Bryn either, and Wren knew, the way you know the moment before a horse shies, that something was already loose in the room.

'The wool,' Bryn said, 'goes to Fallow Cross, and to the villages under the fell. It doesn't go to Carrow. Carrow's a market town under a hill with nothing on the hill but bog and fog and old holes in the ground, and no man takes wool there when Fallow Cross is nearer.' She looked at Ash. 'So I asked him, on the way in, before you came down. And he told me.'
Wren turned on the bench. Ash had his hat up against his chest, both hands on the brim, and the thin pink line down his cheek stood out pale against the brown of him, and he was looking at the table.
'He told you what,' Wren said.

'That there's silver under that fell,' Bryn said. 'Worked once, and forgotten, and the old levels run further than the grant says they do, and there's a survey of it in the case, and there's a man in this town who'd pay to see it never go on a record.'

Wren stood up. The bench went back with a scrape on the flags and the carters by the window turned round to look and Sela looked up and looked down again and went on with her pouring. Wren did not care. She got the case up off the floor and tucked it under her arm and walked out through the doorway into the yard, and the yard was bright and hot and full of the smell of the middens and the cattle market and she stood in the middle of it with her arm aching and her heart going and wanted very much to hit something.
Ash came out after her. He had his hat in his hand and he stopped a few feet off, which was a thing he did, standing off and letting her come to it, and she hated that too.
'You promised,' she said.
'I know it.'
'You promised me in the bothy, on the hill, with the fire going. You said nothing to anyone, ever. Those were the words.'
'I know the words.' He turned the hat round. 'Wren—'
'She's your cousin. That's not the same as you.'

'She's my cousin and she's a carter and she's got a cart going west the day after tomorrow with two places on it, and I wanted—' He stopped and started again. 'I wanted her to take us because I asked her to, and not because she's doing me a favour and wondering the whole way why I'm asking. Bryn doesn't carry people she can't make sense of. She'd have put us off the cart at the town gate and gone on.'
'So you spent my secret for a seat.'
'I spent it,' Ash said, 'for the seat, and I'd do it again, and you can be as angry as you like about it and I'll stand here and take it.'
'That's very handsome.'
'It isn't handsome. It's the truth. I'm no good at the other thing.'

Wren stood in the yard and looked at him. There was a red mark on the cobbles where somebody had tipped a bucket, and a goose was working along the wall with its neck out, and the lamp above the door was unlit and would be lit at dusk. Seventeen days. The case under her arm, and the seal in it, and a dead man's survey, and now a carter from Harrowgate knew what was in it.
'You'll not do it again,' she said.
'No.'
'You'll not say another word to anyone in this town, not to her, not to Sela, not to a man in the street who asks you the time.'
'No.'
'Then get out of my road,' Wren said, 'I'm going back in.'

Bryn had not moved. She was sitting with her back to the wall and her hands folded on the table and her cup turned a quarter-turn, and she watched Wren come back across the floor and sit down on the bench with the case between her feet, and she waited, which was somehow worse than being asked.
'He shouldn't have told you,' Wren said.

'No,' Bryn said. 'He shouldn't. He's always been like that. He was like that at ten years old, and he'll be like that at fifty, and my aunt used to say it was a wonder he got through a winter alive.' She looked past Wren to the door, where Ash had come in and stopped and was standing with his hat in his hand, not sitting. 'Well,' Bryn said to him. 'Sit down, then. You've made your bed.'
Ash sat.

'Now,' Bryn said, and she turned her cup again, and she looked at Wren with her flat, unhurried eyes, and there was no softness in it, but there was no appetite in it either, no leaning forward, no gleam, nothing Wren had seen in Gale's face on the step of Edric's house with the gold in his hand. 'Silver under the fell. That's a thing men kill each other for, and I've no interest in it. I'm a farrier and a carter, and I shoe horses and I carry loads, and I have never in thirty-four years in this town wanted a hill. I want to know one thing and then I'm done asking. Who's the man?'
'You don't need the name,' Wren said.
'I do, if he's on the road west.'
'He isn't. He's behind us and he'll stay behind us, and if he doesn't, the name won't help you.'
Bryn thought about that. She turned her cup. Then she moved the cup off to one side and put her hand flat on the table, and the old white burn scar across the back of it caught the light.

'Then here's what I'll say,' she said. 'Day after tomorrow I load salt fish and dyed cloth onto the cart and I go out the west gate and up the Fallow Cross road, and there's two places under the canvas. It's slow. It's covered. Nobody looks under a carter's canvas, because carters smell of fish. You and him. Both.'

Wren looked at the case between her feet. She thought about the forty miles, and the seventeen days, and the grey-coated man walking south down the lane with his hat in his hand and no mud on him. She thought about the road out of Harrowgate going west with canvas over her head and the smell of salt fish in her nose the whole way, and about the man beside her who talked too much and had put a knife on his own face for her, and who had just spent the one thing she had, and had done it, she thought, roughly the way she would have done it herself if she had been the one who could talk to people.
'One thing,' Wren said. 'The case doesn't leave my hands. Not the cart, not the barn, not the night. If it goes in the cart, it goes in my hands.'
Bryn looked at her a while longer.

'That's the way I'd carry it,' she said. She stood up and picked her apron off the bench with one hand and shook it out and put it on, and took up the coiled whip, and looked down at Ash. 'Fallow Cross road, west gate, first light. If you're not there I'll not wait, and I'll not come back for you, and I'll say I never had a cousin.' She looked at Wren. 'Girl. Bring your case.'
She went out through the door into the lane, unhurried, and the light took her.

Ash sat with his hat in his lap and did not say anything. Sela came over and picked up Bryn's cup and looked at the two of them and said nothing either, which for Sela was an act of great restraint, and went away again.
Wren pulled the case up onto her knees and put both hands on it.
'Two days,' she said.

scenes.title: Gale's offer

beats: Gale finds Wren alone in the inn yard and offers twenty crowns for "the old man’s papers".
He does not say what is in them, and Wren sees he does not know.
She refuses; he smiles and says there is time.

paragraphs: Sela lit the lamp above the yard door at dusk, and Wren went out to the privy with the case under her arm because she was not going to leave it on the bench for anyone, not even for the length of the yard.
Coming back, she stopped.

A man stood by the mounting block with his hat in his hand. Grey coat, good cloth, no mud on the boots. He was looking up at the windows of the inn as though he were pricing the slates, and he did not turn until she was four paces off, and then he turned the way a man turns when he has heard you the whole time.
‘Mistress Hollis,’ Gale said.

She kept walking. If she stopped in the open yard she would have to stand there, and if she ran he would see her run. She put her back to the wall beside the door, where the stone was still holding the day's heat, and set the case down against her leg.
‘You have the advantage of me,’ she said.

‘Gale.’ He inclined his head. ‘We have not been introduced. I called at a house in Linmouth with my hat in my hand and the door open, and a young woman told me her master was dead, and I have thought about that young woman a good deal since.’
‘There's no one of that name here.’

‘There is,’ he said, mildly. ‘The innkeeper has a girl under her roof from Linmouth. Small. Reddish hair. She did not wake you, when I asked, because she said you were a wool buyer and abed with your samples and books, and I am a courteous man, so I went away.’ He turned his hat a quarter turn in his hands and turned it back. ‘I am not a fool, though. There is no wool worth carrying in a brass-cornered surveyor's case, and wool buyers do not go about Harrowgate with their left sleeve burned off at the wrist.’

The lamp above the door threw a yellow bar across the cobbles between them. Wren heard the taproom behind her, a man laughing, a bench leg scraping. Ten feet and a wall of stone between her and all of that.
‘You’ve had your walk for nothing, then,’ she said.

‘I think not.’ Gale looked at the case, unhurried, the way a man looks at a horse he means to buy and has not yet decided to praise. ‘I’ll say it plainly, and you may take it or leave it. Twenty crowns. For the old man's papers. Whatever is in the case, and whatever is not. Twenty crowns, in gold, tonight, in your hand, and I carry the case out of Harrowgate myself and you never see me or it again.’

Twenty crowns, Wren thought. She had sold her grandfather's watch for five shillings. Twenty crowns was two hundred and forty shillings. It was more than Edric had paid her in three years, and Edric had kept her wages short on purpose, to buy her the time.
She looked at Gale's face while she thought it, and what she saw there was the thing that decided her.
He was waiting. He was patient, and he was pleasant, and he had the money, and he did not know.

He had said the old man's papers. Not the survey. Not the fell. Not the levels, not the grant, not a word of what was written in the field books or why a warden of the western fells would want a hill he did not own. He had come to the burnt house and offered gold for papers, and now he stood in the yard of an inn in Harrowgate with his hat in his hand and offered gold for papers, and he had never once said what was in them. If he knew, he would have said it. Men who know say the name of the thing they are buying; that is how they make you understand the price is fair. He did not know. He had been sent for the case and he was fetching the case, and the case was a box to him, and somewhere behind him Warden Vey was keeping his own counsel about what the box was worth.
‘No,’ Wren said.
‘Twenty crowns is a great deal of money for a girl who sold a watch to buy a horse.’
‘It is,’ she said. ‘The answer’s no.’
‘May I ask why?’
‘You may ask.’

Gale smiled. It was a good smile, practised, and it did not reach as far as his eyes, and it did not need to. ‘Your master was a careful man,’ he said. ‘Careful men keep copies. And careful apprentices know where. I would rather buy from you than take it off you, Mistress Hollis. I mean that as a courtesy, not a threat. It is simply true that one of those two things is easier for both of us, and I would prefer the easier one, and I am in no hurry at all.’
There it was. Wren kept her hands at her sides and her eyes on his collar, because if she looked at the case he would look at the case.

‘My master is dead,’ she said. ‘He died in that chair. There was nothing in the house to sell you, and there is nothing here. If you want papers, go to the assay office. They keep ledgers. I hear they are very good at writing things down.’
‘I have been to the assay office,’ Gale said.

That stopped her for the space of a breath, and she was angry with herself for it, and she let it show on her face as nothing. He had been to the assay office. Of course he had. The clerk with his sleeve pinned back and his sour mouth and his pen that stopped when she said Edric Rone—the clerk had written nothing down, and he had looked at her, and Gale had been in that room or would be in it, and the clerk would remember the girl who came asking after a dead surveyor's Carrow papers whether he wrote it down or not.

‘Then you know what they told me,’ she said. ‘Surveys go before the Assize. Not to clerks. Not to wardens’ men. Before the Assize, in person, and there is a long road to Carrow and I am not walking it for anybody but the man who made the survey.’
Gale put his hat on his head and took it off again, slowly, as though he had remembered something and then thought better of it.
‘There is time,’ he said.
‘There isn’t much.’

‘There is more than you think.’ He stepped back off the mounting block and gave her the whole yard. ‘You will be at the market tomorrow. And the day after. And the day after that, perhaps, if the weather holds, and it will hold; they say it has been dry nine days and there is no rain in it yet. I am lodging in this town. I am not hard to find, and I am not in the habit of hurrying people. Twenty crowns stands until it does not.’
‘It can stand till midsummer.’

‘Midsummer,’ Gale said, and something moved behind his pleasant face, some small private arithmetic being done and found satisfactory. ‘Yes. I had heard the Assize sits at midsummer. Goodnight, Mistress Hollis. Mind the arm. A burn wants air, they tell me, but not this much sun.’

He walked off down the lane towards the river, unhurried, hat in hand, and did not look back at her, and the yellow bar of the lamp did not reach far enough to follow him. Wren stood against the wall until the sound of his boots had gone out of the lane and into the general noise of the town, and then she picked up the case and held it against her chest with both arms, and found that her hands were shaking, and found that she did not care that they were.
Twenty crowns. He did not know what was in it.

She had said two days to Ash, in the taproom, with the cup still on the table where Bryn had left it. She went back in through the door and along the room to the bench by the chimney, and she sat down with the case on her knees, and when Ash looked up from his hat she shook her head once, small, and he did not ask her anything in front of Sela, and she sat there and counted the days again from the beginning, slowly, the way she counted cattle, because counting was the only thing she had ever been able to do that made a thing more true.
Seventeen.

scenes.title: The west gate

beats: They leave Harrowgate before dawn, Bryn driving her cart, Ash and Wren riding beside it.
Bryn decides they will go back by the Linn ferry, not the Carrow road where Gale will watch.
The city falls behind them.

paragraphs: Wren woke before the bell, in the dark, with her boots on.

She had not meant to sleep. She had meant to sit up the way she had sat up the night before, her back to the wall and the case in her lap, and count the hours down. But somewhere in the small hours the counting had gone soft at the edges, and she came awake with her cheek against the case and her neck stiff and the window showing grey, and she was up and had the strap over her shoulder before she had properly decided anything.
Ash was in the yard. He had Cinder by the halter and both horses saddled, and he was doing something to a girth strap with his thumb, and he did not say good morning, and she did not say it either.
‘Bryn?’
‘Coming round the back.’ He nodded at the arch. ‘She won’t come through the house. Says she won’t wake the woman and have to talk to her.’
That was Bryn all over, Wren thought, and it was the first thing about her she had liked without reservation.

They went out through the stable arch into the lane at the back, where the cart stood already loaded and sheeted, the shafts up and the horse between them stamping at the flies. It smelled of salt fish, that cold briny smell that gets into cloth and stays. Bryn was at the tail of the cart, checking the lashings with one hand, her whip coiled at her belt. She looked them over once, the way she looked over everything, and swung up onto the box.
‘Get on,’ she said. ‘The gate opens at four and there’s a queue of carts at it that were there before me.’

Wren mounted Cinder. Her arm complained, the way it complained every morning now, a deep pull from wrist to elbow and a sting where the bandage had shifted in the night. She took the reins in her right hand and kept the left inside her coat, and turned the grey gelding in behind the cart.

Harrowgate was not a city that slept. Even at this hour the lane had life in it: a boy going by with a yoke of water cans, a woman setting out a board of bread on two trestles, a dog asleep against the wall that lifted its head and put it down again. But the market was a different place than it had been at noon, all the shouting drawn out of it, the pens empty and hosed down, the cobbles black and shining. They went along the market wall and up the hill towards the west gate, and the cart wheels rang on the stone, and nobody said anything.

The gatehouse stood at the top, with its two towers and its arch, and a lantern burning in the arch though the sky behind it had begun to go the colour of a knife. Two carts were ahead of them in the queue. The gatekeeper came out from his little door with a board, and the first carter gave his name and his load and paid, and then the second, and then Bryn.

‘Bryn Tally. Salt fish and dyed cloth. Fallow Cross and the villages under the fell.’ She put the coins on the board without being asked, and the gatekeeper counted them and nodded and chalked something and went back into his door.
‘You didn’t say two riders,’ Wren said, when they were through and out on the road.
‘I didn’t say no riders either,’ Bryn said. ‘He knows me. He knows I don’t carry people I don’t know where they’re going, and he doesn’t want to know where I carry them. That’s the arrangement.’

The road ran west out of the gate along the top of the ridge, and below them to the left the town lay in its wall, the roofs going grey and then gold as the sun came up over the far side, and the river a pale line away south. There was smoke from the chimneys, thin and straight, because there had been no wind for ten days and the sky was clear as a bowl. Wren looked back once, at the gatehouse and the wall and the roofs, and thought about Gale somewhere down there in a good grey coat, in a lodging he was not hard to find at, and about the seventeen days, and she did not look back again.

They went on a mile or so without speaking, the cart jolting, Cinder stepping out well enough on the level. Ash rode on the off side with his hat down against the light, and it was he who said, at last, the thing Wren had been waiting for one of them to say.
‘You’re going the wrong road for Carrow.’
Bryn did not turn her head. ‘I know what road I’m on.’
‘We want west,’ Ash said. ‘Carrow’s south and east of here. The Carrow road runs out of the south gate and it’s a good road and it goes where we’re going.’

‘It goes where you’re going,’ Bryn said, and spat over the side of the cart. ‘It also goes past the bridge, and the bridge has a man on it, or will have, if your grey-coated friend is half the man you think he is. There’s one road out of the south gate. One. You put a man on it and he sees everything that goes down it and he writes it in a book and shows it to whoever pays him. I’ve carted twenty years and I know how a man is watched for.’
‘So we go west,’ Ash said.

‘We go west.’ She shifted the reins in her hands. ‘Two days to Fallow Cross and the villages. Then I turn south at the fen and come back east by the Linn. There’s a ferry below Linmouth, a rope on two posts, and the man who keeps it takes anyone with two coppers and asks nothing. From the ferry it’s a day’s ride up to the salt road and the salt road runs south to Carrow. You come at Carrow from the west and nobody’s looking west, because nobody comes west. It’s four days round instead of two, and it’s the way I’d go, and if you don’t like it you can get down here and walk down the south road with your hat over your face and see how far that gets you.’
Ash looked across at Wren.

Wren thought about it. Four days round, and the days were seventeen and going down like water out of a cracked pail. Four days was a great deal. But she had seen Gale in the yard with his hat in his hand, saying there is time, saying it the way a man says a thing he has already written down, and she had spent the whole night with that sentence in her head, and she knew what it meant. It meant let her run. It meant the south road, and the bridge, and a man with a book.
‘The ferry,’ she said.
Ash nodded, slow. He had the grace not to argue it, and she gave him that much.

The sun came up properly and the road went on west, and the town fell away behind them until it was nothing but a smudge of smoke on the sky and then not even that. The land opened out into long fields with hawthorn hedges, and larks going up over them and dropping again, and the cart creaked and the horse leaned into the collar and the wheels turned over and over on the dry road. Wren loosened her coat because of the heat and then drew it back over the bandage, and kept the case on the saddle in front of her, one hand on the strap.

They did not talk much. Ash told one story about a horse that would only drink out of a hat, and Bryn said she had known the horse, and that was the end of that. A carter coming east passed them with a load of hurdles and lifted two fingers off the rein, and Bryn lifted two back. The sun rose and the day got hot, and the dust came off the wheels in a long slow plume behind them, hanging in the still air because there was no wind in it, none at all.
Wren counted the days again, from the beginning, the way she counted cattle. Seventeen.

scenes.title: The toll again

beats: They cross Haldon Bridge again.
Bryn haggles with Mother Agate and pays for all of them.
Mother Agate cackles that she has never had such a good toll as last time.

paragraphs: They came on the bridge in the middle of the second morning, and Wren knew the place before she saw the water: the three grey arches, the parapet worn round as a rope, the river going under brown and quick with the spring melt. She had crossed it going the other way eight days ago and paid for it with her grandmother's compass, and the whole of it came back to her at once, the stool, the stick, the coat the colour of the road.
Bryn brought the cart down to the narrow place and stopped it square, and the horse put its head down and blew.
Mother Agate was where she had been, on the near side, stick across her knees, hands folded on the stick. She looked at the cart, the horse, the two riders, and she did not get up.
'Toll,' she said.
'Aye,' said Bryn.
'What's your load?'
'Salt fish and dyed cloth for Fallow Cross and the villages under the fell.'
'And the two on the horses?'
'Passengers.'

Agate looked at Ash a while, at the thin pink line down his cheek, and then at Wren, and Wren saw her eyes go to the coat, the left sleeve of it, the way Wren kept that arm inside. The old woman's face did not move.
'Penny a beast, penny the rider,' she said. 'The dog goes free.'
'There's no dog,' said Bryn.
'Then there's no free dog,' Agate said. 'Two riders, two horses, one cart, one horse in the shafts, and the cart's a beast when it's loaded. Sixpence.'
'Four.'
'Sixpence.'
Bryn reached into the purse at her belt, unhurried, and counted the coins into her palm and held them out. 'Six, then. For all of us.'
Agate took them and put them somewhere inside the man's coat and did not count them again. That was the whole of the haggling, and it was over.

Wren sat Cinder with her hand on the case strap, and she was already looking past the old woman at the far bank, at the road going up out of the willows, when Agate turned her head and looked at her the way she had looked at her before, and then reached up with both knotted hands and pulled something out from the neck of the coat, on a cord.
It was the compass.

The brass was polished by the wearing of it, and the cord was a length of tarred line, and it hung against the old woman's chest where anybody coming over the bridge could see it, and Agate let it lie there on the outside of the coat with her hand still on it, thumb on the lid.

She looked at Wren and her mouth moved, and Wren thought she was going to say something about the price, the way she had said it before, the way she had asked whether she was a surveyor and made her pay in the one coin that mattered.
Instead she laughed.
It came out of her small and dry and it went on longer than Wren expected, and she rocked back on the stool with it, both hands on the stick, and the compass swung on its cord against her chest.

'Ten years,' she said, when she had it out of her. 'Ten years I've sat this bridge and I've had pennies and I've had a hen and once a man's boots, and I never had such a toll as I had off you, girl. Never such a toll.'
'It's brass,' Wren said.

'It's brass,' Agate agreed, cheerful, wiping her eyes with the flat of her hand. 'And it's a better thing than any sixpence that ever came over my bridge, and I've had it out every day since, and it reads true, and you'll not get it back for sixpence or six pounds either one.'
'I know it,' Wren said.
'You do,' said Agate. 'That's why it was worth the taking.'

Bryn clicked her tongue and the cart horse leaned into the collar and the cart moved, and the wheels went up onto the stone, and Ash rode after it with his hat in his lap. Wren gathered the reins. Cinder stepped out onto the bridge, and the sound of the hooves came up off the stone and off the water together, doubled and hollow, and under them the river ran brown and fast with the melt.

She did not look back at the old woman, and she did not look down at the cord and the brass swinging over the man's coat. She kept her eyes on the far bank and the road going up out of the willows, and she counted, without meaning to, the days: sixteen. Then she counted the arches as Cinder crossed them, the way she counted anything that could be counted, because there was no sense in looking at a thing you could not have back.

On the far side the road bent up between hedges, and the dust came off the wheels in a long slow plume and hung in the still air behind them, and there was no wind in it, none at all. Ash rode up level with her, on the off side of the cart, and did not say anything about the compass. He had seen it. He had the grace, at least, not to say anything about it.
Behind them Mother Agate sat on her stool with the stick across her knees and the brass compass shining on the outside of her coat, and waited for the next of them.

scenes.title: A cast shoe

beats: Rain on the Drove Road.
Wren’s horse casts a shoe; Bryn shoes him at the roadside from her cart’s tools.
Bryn and Wren talk properly for the first time.

paragraphs: Rain came down on the Drove Road the way it came down in the cloud country, not in drops but in a grey sheet that moved across the valley and took the hills out one behind another. It started before noon on the second day, while the sun was still on them, so that the dust under the wheels turned to a smell and the dust in the air turned to mud in the nose, and then the sun went and there was only the rain and the road.

Wren had her hat down and her collar up and the case under the front of her coat with the flap over it, and inside ten minutes she was wet through the shoulders and the rain was running off the brim in a line down the back of her neck. Cinder put his head down to it and walked.

Bryn's cart had a canvas over the salt fish, tied along the rails, and the rain beat a flat drum on it for miles. Ash rode with his hat held over the saddle horn as though it were the horse that needed the shelter, and after a while he gave that up and put the hat on.

The road came down off the shoulder of the hill and into the top of a long valley, and the rain thinned to a drizzle and then to nothing, and the clouds went over and left the wet hillside steaming in the sun. They stopped where the road levelled by a stand of thorn and let the horses put their heads down.

Wren swung off Cinder and felt it in her legs at once, the stiffness after two days of walking him through weather, and she went round him with her hand along his flank, and that was when she saw it. The off hind was shod three ways and bare on the fourth. The shoe was gone. He had cast it somewhere up the hill, in the rain, and she had not felt it in the saddle and he had not faltered and there was nothing in the mud behind them now but the road.
'Bryn,' she said.

Bryn was already down off the box and coming round the cart with her apron swinging. She looked at the foot without touching it, then took the foot up and turned it and looked at the hoof wall, and put it down.
'When?'
'Somewhere back. I don't know.'
'You'd not know,' Bryn said. 'He's not the sort to tell you.' She straightened. 'It's a clean cast, no split. I'll put it back on.'
'You've a forge in that cart?'

Bryn gave her a look that had no hurry in it at all. 'I've a forge in every cart I've ever had, girl. You don't cart twenty years and wait on a smith at the roadside.' She went to the tail of the cart and pulled the pins and let the board down, and inside, under the canvas and lashed against the salt fish, was a small anvil and a hammer and a box of nails and pincers and a pair of tongs, and a leather apron folded over the lot.
Ash came and took Cinder's head and stood with him, talking nonsense into his ear, and the gelding stood for it and only once tried to walk over the top of him to see what was in the cart.

Bryn built a fire in the lee of the bank from dry thorn she pulled out of the hedge bottom, and she had Cinder's foot up on her knee and the old nails out and the hoof pared and the shoe hot off the little fire and set on before the kettle would have boiled. The smoke blew away down the valley. The smell of it, hot iron and burnt horn, was the first smell in two days that belonged to work rather than weather.
'He's a good foot,' Bryn said, working the nails. 'Whoever shod him last knew what he was at. That's not Hobb.'
'Ash bought him off Hobb.'
'I know what Ash bought off Hobb. I'm saying the shoe came from somewhere better than Hobb.' She set the last nail and clenched it and ran her thumb along the wall. 'There. He'll go.'
Wren got the money out of her jumper pocket. 'What do I owe you?'
'For a shoe and a fire at the roadside?'
'For the shoe and the fire and the tools and the cart.'
Bryn looked at the coins for a moment and then took one, the smallest, and put it in her apron pocket, and started knocking the fire apart with the toe of her boot.
Wren stood there with the rest of it in her hand. She had not expected to be charged nothing and she had not expected to be charged a penny, and she did not know yet which of those it was.

They let the horses graze a while, because the rain had brought the grass up and there was no hurry in the day that Bryn would admit to. Ash lay back on the bank with his hat over his face and was asleep in the time it would take to count to sixty. Wren sat on the cart step with the case across her knees and watched the water standing in the ruts go down as it soaked away.
Bryn came and sat on the box above her, not beside her, and took the coiled whip off her belt and began to run tallow through the fall of it, unhurried, thumb and forefinger, the length of it.
'You've not asked me anything,' Wren said.
'You've not told me anything,' Bryn said. 'Different thing.'
'Ash told you.'

'Ash told me a piece of it on the way in, and I've had the rest off my own eyes since, which is how I'd rather have it.' She pulled another length of the fall through her hand and held it up to the light and found nothing wrong with it. 'You keep a brass-cornered case in both hands and you sleep on it and you've an arm under that bandage that a fire made, and you're bound for Carrow when the wool trade runs west. I don't need the whole of it.'
'And you're carrying me anyway.'
'I'm carrying Ash,' Bryn said. 'You come with him. That's how it works.'
Wren turned that over. It was the plainest thing anyone had said to her since the door gave way in Linmouth, and she found she did not mind it.
'He told you about the fell,' she said.
'He told me there's silver under it.'

'There is. There's silver under it and it's on the record books nowhere, and there's a man in Harrowgate who'd pay to keep it that way.' She looked at the wet road. 'That's the whole of it. What Ash didn't say is that it's my master's work, and he's dead, and I'm the one who has to lay it. If I don't get it before the Assize rises, it's a year, and a year is long enough for a man like that to take the fell out from under the town.'
Bryn ran the fall through her hand again and did not look up at her.
'How long since your master died?'
'Nine days.'
'And you've come through the fire and the ferry and the fair and the bridge and the two men in the wood,' Bryn said, 'and you're sat here asking me what you owe me for a shoe.'
Wren did not answer that.

Bryn coiled the whip and hung it back on her belt and looked down the valley at the road going away from them into the low ground, and then she said, without any change in her voice, 'I've a brother at Carrow. Went to his wife's people twelve year back and took the strong arm of the family with him. I've not seen him since the wedding.' She got down off the box. 'So there's two of us has business at Carrow and only one of us that says so.'
'Wren,' Wren said. 'Wren Hollis.'
'I know it. It's all over Sela's walls by now.' Bryn took the nosebag off the cart horse and put it on him. 'Get your grey up. The fen's a day and a half and I'd rather cross it in the light.'

They went on down out of the thorn and into the valley and the road ran pale and drying in the sun, and the water went up off the land in a haze that made the far shoulder of the hill move as you looked at it. Ash woke up singing something that was mostly about a girl and not much about a tune, and Cinder stepped out on the new shoe as if he had never lost it.

scenes.title: The paddock

beats: They pass Hobb's Farm.
Wren goes to the paddock fence to see her mare.
She decides to leave her there until she can come back for her.

paragraphs: The valley road ran down through wet grass and came out on the shoulder of the hill above the farm, and from up there Wren could see the whole of it — the long grey house with the byre at one end, the peat stack against the gable, the small field below the road where a grey gelding had stood the day Ash bought him. Smoke went up thin and straight from the chimney. The rain had stopped an hour back and the sun had come out, and the roof steamed.

Bryn drew the cart to a halt in the widening where the track turned down to the farm. She did not say anything. She put the brake on and took out her pipe and began to fill it, looking away down the valley, giving Wren the road and the turning and the choice of it without putting a word to any of it.
Ash had stopped his singing. He sat on the off side of the cart with his hat pushed back, watching the field.
'You'll not be long,' he said. It was not a question.

Wren got down off Cinder and led him off the road onto the trodden ground at the gate. Her legs were stiff from two days in the saddle after two days of walking, and she went the first few steps like an old woman before they came back to her. She tied the reins to the gatepost, loose enough that the grey could put his head down, and he did, at once, into the wet grass, and stayed there.

The field gate was open. She went through it and along the wall to the paddock beside the byre, where the ground was beaten flat and there was a rack of hay and a water butt and the smell of cattle coming through the byre wall, warm and close. Thistle stood at the far side with her head down and one hip cocked, the way she had stood at the horse fair at Fallow Cross, taking no particular interest in anything. There was a poultice bound on her off fore, wrapped in sacking and tied at the fetlock with cord. When Wren came to the fence she lifted her head and looked, and then went back to the hay.

Wren put her hand over the rail. The mare came across, unhurried, and put her nose against Wren's knuckles and stood there, breathing. Wren rubbed the flat of her hand up the long plain face and under the black forelock and along the jaw, where the winter coat was still coming out in handfuls, and the mare leaned into it and closed her eyes.

The off fore was set down square and the toe rested. Wren crouched at the rail and looked at it. The coronet was still a little full, but not the way it had been — the heat had gone out of it, and the leg above it was down to its proper size. The farmer's wife had done what she said she would do.
'She's not for riding,' the woman said.
She had come out of the byre with a bucket and stood on the other side of the fence, a short woman in a coat the colour of the byre wall, looking at the mare's foot and then at Wren.
'No,' Wren said.

'Another week and I'll take the poultice off and turn her out. Then another week on the grass and she can be walked.' She set the bucket down. 'You said a fortnight. I'll keep her a fortnight more if you've a mind. Two shillings the same.'

Wren looked at the mare. Then she put her hand back inside her jumper, where the purse sat in the pocket with the broken button and the watch chain and nothing else. There had been a shilling and fourpence in it when she left Harrowgate. There was fourpence now, and Bryn had taken one penny of that for the shoe and the fire yesterday and given her the rest back in change, which was to say she had not taken it at all.
'Two shillings when I come back,' Wren said. 'The way it was.'
'That's what I said.'
'And she's not to be sold, nor lent, nor put to the cart.'
The woman looked at her a while. 'You said that too.'
'I know it.'
'Then it's said,' the woman said, and picked up her bucket and went back into the byre, and the dark took her.

Wren stood at the rail. She put her hand out and the mare came back to it and stood, and Wren rubbed the white fleck on her forehead with her thumb, round and round, the way she had done at the bothy when there was nothing else to do in the evening but sit with her and let the fire go down. The mare's breath came warm onto her wrist and the wet of it dried.

'You'll have grass,' Wren said, quiet enough that it was for the mare and not for anyone else. 'You'll have the box when it rains. You'll have her, and she'll do it right, and she'll not sell you.' She smoothed the black mane down flat on both sides of the neck. 'I've to go on. I'll come back for you. I said it and I'll do it.'
The mare put her head down and pulled at the hay in the rack, and that was the whole of her answer, and Wren found she was glad of it. A horse that made a fuss would have been worse.
She took her hand off the rail, and went back across the field, and out through the gate, and shut it behind her, and latched it.

Ash had got down off the cart and was standing at Cinder's head, holding the reins. He had not come over to the fence, and he did not say anything now. He only gave her the reins and put his foot in the stirrup and got up behind the saddle as she mounted, sitting on the cantle with his hands on the skirt, light as a boy.

Bryn had her pipe going. She looked at Wren once, up and down, taking in the face and the hands and the way she sat the grey, and then she knocked the pipe out on the box and put it away and took up the reins.
'Two shillings,' she said. 'You've got the price of it in your head or you've not.'
'It's in my head,' Wren said.

'Then that's settled.' Bryn let the brake off and the cart moved, and the horse leaned into the collar and the wheels turned up out of the widening onto the road. 'The fen's a day and a half and the light's going. Walk him on.'

Wren turned Cinder's head down the road, and the grey went forward on the new shoe without being asked twice, stepping out long and even, as if he had never lost it and never meant to. She looked back once, over her shoulder, and the paddock was behind the byre wall from there and there was nothing to see but the grey house and the smoke and the wet field steaming in the sun.
She kept the case on the saddle in front of her, under her hand. Fourteen days to midsummer. The road went down into the low ground and away, and she rode after the cart.

scenes.title: The ford

beats: Gale and two riders wait at a ford.
Gale calls Wren by her real name and her master’s name; the wool-buyer story is finished.
Bryn drives the cart straight through the ford and they get away.

paragraphs: They came down off the shoulder in the last of the light and the road ran out flat across the low ground, and Wren saw the ford before she saw the men: water lying across the stones in a wide brown sheet, and three horses standing on the far bank with their heads down, drinking.
She counted them without meaning to. Three. Two with saddles and a third with a saddle and a led rein, and a man standing in the shallows with his boots in the water, holding his hat.
Ash's hand came up onto her shoulder and stayed there.
'Keep going,' he said, low, at her ear. 'Bryn's driving on.'

Bryn was. The cart did not slow. Wren could see her on the box with the reins in her fists and her shoulders squared to the water, and the horse in the shafts had its head down already, feeling for the stones, and the wheels went in with a noise like a long breath let out.
The man in the shallows put his hat on.
'Good evening,' Gale said.

He said it across the water, unhurried, the way a man greets a neighbour at his own gate. He did not step forward. The two riders on the bank did not move either, and their horses went on drinking, and that was the worst of it — the whole of it arranged so that nobody would have to do anything at all.

Bryn's cart was halfway across. The water came up to the axle and boiled round the wheels, and the load under the canvas shifted and settled, and Bryn never looked at the man. She looked at the far bank and the road out of it and the horse's ears.
'You'll be Mistress Hollis,' Gale said.

Wren's hand closed on the case. It was already under her hand, it had been under her hand for two days, and still her fingers tightened on the near strap until the scorched edge of it bit into her palm.
'You're mistaken,' she said.

'I don't think I am.' He had a pleasant face and he used it slowly, the way he used everything. 'I saw you at your master's door in Linmouth. You were carrying a lamp and you told me there was nothing in the house to sell. I remember the hands.' His eyes went down to her left arm, into her coat, and came back up. 'You've been burned.'
'A kitchen fire.'

'Edric Rone's apprentice,' Gale said, 'has a burn from her wrist to her elbow, and carries a brass-cornered case with a scorched strap. I have been a fortnight learning to say your name, mistress. I would rather not have had to.'
Behind her, Ash had not moved. She could feel the weight of him on the cantle, the heat of him through the coat, and the small shift of his boot as he found his balance on the off side.

The cart came up out of the ford with a suck of mud and the wheels found the road and the horse leaned in and Bryn never stopped it. She took it twenty yards up the bank and then she pulled up, square across the road, and sat on the box with the reins slack in her hands, watching, the way she watched a room.

'Twenty crowns,' Gale said. 'The offer stands. It stood in Harrowgate and it stands here, and I'll say the same thing to you that I said then — I'd rather buy from you than take it off you. You're cold and you're tired and you've a long road in front of you and no money that I can see. Give me the case and it's done. Nobody follows you anywhere.'

The water went over the stones at her horse's feet. Cinder put his head down and drank, and she let him, because pulling his head up would have told the man something, and because she needed the moment.
'You've been at the assay office,' she said.
'Yes.'
'And they told you what I am.'

'They told me who your master was,' Gale said. 'They were careful about it. It's a name that makes clerks put their pens down. That is the whole of what I have, and I am content with it.' He shifted his weight in the water, and the current moved round his boots. 'Whatever the old man left in that case, I don't know it and I don't need to. I'm not the one who wants it, mistress. I'm only the one sent to fetch it, which is a much smaller thing to be, and much easier to satisfy.'
