There it was, then, and she had it plain at last: he had not been told. Somewhere behind him a warden sat with his mouth shut, and Gale had ridden sixteen days on the strength of a name and a case and a burned arm, and he did not know what he was carrying.
It did not help her much. He would find out at Carrow, or he would not, and either way he was standing in the ford.
'It's brass,' Wren said. 'And it's not worth a penny to anyone but me.'
'Then you'll not mind parting with it.'
'I'll mind.'
'Bryn,' Ash said, quiet, behind her.

Bryn had already taken up the reins. She looked down the road at the two riders on the bank and at the man in the water, and she spat over the side of the box into the river, and she said, 'There's a load of salt fish on this cart and it's going to Fallow Cross and it's going tonight.'

'You'll wait,' Gale said, and for the first time there was something under the courtesy, a thin hard edge of it, and he took one step forward out of the shallows. 'Mistress Tally, I know your name too, and I know your cart, and I know you run salt fish and dyed cloth and whatever else pays. I've no quarrel with you. Leave the girl and the case on the bank and drive on, and no one will ever ask you what you carried west, and you'll not lose a day.'
Bryn looked at him. It was not a long look. It was the look she gave a horse that would not stand for shoeing.
'You're standing in the road,' she said.
And she hit the horse.

The cart lurched and the shaft horse threw its weight into the collar and the wheels came round and Bryn drove it straight down the bank and into the ford, right at him, with the whole loaded weight of it behind the shod hooves and the iron tyres, and the water went up in a sheet.

Gale got out of it. He had to. He went sideways with his boots slipping on the stones and his hat off and one of the riders shouted and hauled his horse round, and the other one's horse shied back into the second and the three of them came apart in the water like a knot dropped on a table.
'Come on,' Ash said.
Wren put her heels in and Cinder went.

He went into the ford at a trot and the water came up his belly and he did not like it, but the new shoe bit and the stones held, and she kept him at the cart's tail and the cart was already climbing the far bank with the water running off its boards, and behind her the shouting had gone loose and confused and no one had a clear line at her.
She looked back once, at the top of the bank.

Gale stood in the middle of the ford with the water round his knees and his hat in his hand and his good grey coat ruined to the waist, and he was not shouting. He was watching her go. He had the look of a man finishing an account, and when he had finished it he put his hat on, and that was worse than any shout he could have made.
Then the road turned up into the low ground and the cart took it, and the grey went after with his ears forward, and there was nothing behind them but water and the last of the light on it.
Ash let out his breath and sat back.
'He'll have that name of yours from one end of the county by Sunday,' he said.
'He had it already.'
'He didn't have yours.'
'No,' Wren said. 'He has it now.'
She rode on with the case under her hand and the road going grey ahead of them, and somewhere behind the three of them stood in the water and made their arrangements.

scenes.title: Words by the fire

beats: At the night camp Bryn says the claim will make Wren rich and asks for a share; Ash is angry.
Wren says the claim is Edric’s, and hers, and no one’s to sell.
They agree to cross by the Linn ferry and go over the moor to Carrow.

paragraphs: They made three miles in the dark before Bryn turned the cart off the road into a fold of ground where a bank of whin gave some shelter from the west, and there she stopped and put the brake on and got down without a word.

Wren got down too, and found her legs had gone to wood. She walked Cinder out and back along the turf to cool him, then unsaddled and rubbed him down with a handful of grass and left him hobbled where the grazing was good. Ash slid off the cantle and stood holding the saddle with both hands a moment before he lifted it. His face had stiffened on the ride; the pink line under his eye had gone tight and dry at the edges.

Bryn had a fire going by the time the horses were done. She had it out of the cart's own box, kindling and a stub of candle and a handful of dry thorn she must have been carrying since the last one, and she set the kettle on the stones and then sat down on an upturned crate with her back against the wheel, and did not look at either of them.

Nobody said anything for a while. The fire took. The wet ground steamed where the light fell on it, and beyond the circle of it the whin stood black and the sky over the moor had gone the last colour it goes before dark, a greenish grey like a bruise old enough to be losing its colour.
Bryn took her pipe out and filled it from a twist of paper and lit it off a spill and smoked.
Then she said, 'That man knows your name and he knows what you're carrying.'
'He knows there's a case,' Wren said.

'He knows more than that.' Bryn turned the pipe over in her fingers. 'You don't send a man like that after a box of paper. He's been at it a fortnight and he came out to a ford at dark on the off chance. I've carted twenty years. I know how a man is watched for, and I know the other thing too, when a man's been paid past what the errand's worth.' She looked at Wren across the fire, flat and unhurried. 'So. What's it worth?'
Ash said, 'Bryn.'
'I asked the girl.'
'You'll not—'

'I'll ask what I like.' Bryn's eyes did not move off Wren. 'There's silver under that fell. You said it yourself on the road and I've had two days to think on it and I'd be a fool not to. So there's a claim in that case that's worth a deal more than the paper it's written on, and there's a man on this road tonight who'd pay to see it never go on a record, and there's another man behind him who'd pay more. That's a thing worth money, girl. Real money. Not twenty crowns in a purse, not the price of a horse.' She knocked the ash off the pipe against the crate. 'I've carried you four days and I've taken a man's name off him at a ford for you and I've not been paid a penny beyond a shoe. When you lay that claim, I want a share of it.'

'Bryn, for God's sake,' Ash said. He was on his feet, though Wren had not seen him get up. 'She's carrying it for a dead man. You know what that is. You know what it is and you're sitting there with your hand out.'
'I know what it is. I've a forge in every cart I've ever had. That doesn't make me a charity.'
'You've a brother at Carrow and you'd have gone anyway—'

'I'd have gone in the spring and taken the east road and not been wet through at a ford with a gentleman's name in my mouth. Don't tell me what I'd have done.' She said it without heat, which was worse. 'I asked for a share. That's not thieving. That's business, and I'll hear it said to my face.'
Ash turned and walked three steps into the dark and stood with his back to the fire, one hand flat on the back of his neck.

Wren had the case against her knee. She had not put it down since the ford. Her arm ached under the bandage, going down from the elbow in a long slow line, the way it did at night, and she was wet through the shoulders and cold and her legs did not want to hold her, and she thought about Edric at the table with the ink barely dry and about the letter folded inside the case now and about what she had promised him and what she had promised herself at the burned door.
'No,' she said.
Bryn looked at her.

'It's not mine to sell,' Wren said. 'It's his. It's a survey of Carrow Fell made by Edric Rone, sworn surveyor of Linmouth, and it's entered in his name and mine or it isn't entered at all. That's the whole of it. If I take money for it I've sold a dead man's work and I might as well have taken Gale's twenty crowns at the mounting block and gone home. There's no share in it, because there's nothing in it that can be shared. It goes on the record. That's what it's for. That's what he kept my wages short three years for.'
'And after it's on the record?'

'After it's on the record there'll be a fell with silver under it and a town that knows it and a Warden who can't swear it's his. That's all. I don't get rich off that. Nobody does. It just stops being a lie.'
Bryn drew on the pipe and let the smoke out slow through her nose.
'You'll not get rich,' she said. 'You'll be the girl who carried it. That's a poor trade.'
'It's the trade I've got.'
The fire cracked and settled. Somewhere out in the dark one of the cart horses shifted its feet. Ash came back in and sat down on the ground by the kettle and did not look at his cousin.
Bryn took the pipe out of her mouth and looked at the bowl of it a while, and then she put it back in and said, 'Then I'll want the shoe paid for.'
'You've had it.'

'I've had a penny of it.' She said it flat, and then something moved at the corner of her mouth that was not quite a smile and did not last. 'All right, girl. All right. I've carried salt fish for men who'd sell their mothers at the far end of the run, and I'll carry you as far as the fen and no further in the way of argument. But I'll say this and then I'll leave it. When that case goes on the record, there'll be men at Carrow who want to know who carried it and who stood at the ford with you. My name'll be in it. I've a brother there I've not seen twelve years, and I'd sooner not have him hear of me from a Warden's man.'
'He won't hear it from me,' Wren said.
'No,' Bryn said. 'He won't.'

Ash poured the water into the pot and passed it round and they ate bread and a little of the cold bacon without much talk. The moon came up late and small over the moor and made the wet ground shine. Wren rewound the bandage on her arm by firelight, one-handed as she had learned to, and the burn had gone quiet under the grease and the marks of Edric's cuff were still there in the flesh, pale red, like something pressed into wax and left.
After a while Bryn said, without looking up from the fire, 'Where do you mean to cross?'
'The Linn,' Wren said. 'The ferry below Linmouth. Two coppers and the man asks nothing.'
'That's Oskar Venn's boat,' Ash said. 'He'll ask something. He always asks something.'
'He asked me where I was going and I told him. He'll ask again.'
'Then he'll know.'
'He'll know what he knew the first time,' Wren said. 'That I'm a girl with a case, going somewhere east of where I started. That's not a name and it's not a thing worth a man's while.'

Bryn nodded slowly, working it. 'Ferry puts you on the west bank with the salt road running south under your hand. From there it's the moor and down to Carrow, and no bridge and no gate and nobody keeping a book on it. A day and a half if the ground's dry.' She looked at the sky over the whin. 'It won't be dry.'
'Then it'll be two,' Wren said.

'It'll be two.' Bryn got up and knocked the dottle out of her pipe and put it in the pocket of her apron. 'I'll want an early start. If that man's half what you say he is, he'll have a horse under him by morning and he'll know the roads better than I do.'
'He will,' Wren said.
Bryn climbed up into the cart and pulled the canvas over herself and was quiet.

Ash banked the fire with the last of the thorn and lay down with his coat under his head and his hat over his face. Wren sat up a while longer with the case across her knees, listening to the horses and the water in the ground, and then she lay down on her side with the case between her and the fire and her good arm over it, and slept.

They were on the road before first light, the wheels cutting through the wet, and by noon the ground had begun to climb and the beech woods were behind them and the whole moor stood open ahead, brown and grey and going on for ever, and somewhere beyond the far edge of it the river ran and the ferry crossed and the road went south to Carrow, and there were thirteen days.

scenes.title: Ashes

beats: On the hill above Linmouth Wren sees the burned shell of Edric's house.
She goes down alone and stands in the ruin.
Ash comes to find her; she lets herself cry.

paragraphs: They came over the shoulder of the moor in the middle of the afternoon and the whole coast opened below them, the grey water flat to the horizon and the town sitting at the river mouth with its back to the hill. Wren knew it before she could have named a single roof. The smell of it came up on the wind, salt and tar and the burnt-scrub smell of the gorse, and her hands had tightened on the reins before her eyes had found what they were looking for.

The house was the black tooth in the row. Everything else along the terrace still had its roof and its chimney and its windows giving back the light, and where Edric's house had stood there was a shell, the gable ends standing, the slates gone, the whole middle of it fallen in and gone grey with ash and rain. Three weeks of weather had washed the soot down the walls in long streaks, like the house had wept and dried.
'There,' Ash said behind her. He had seen it too. He said nothing else.
The cart had stopped ahead where the track bent toward the town. Bryn sat on the box with the reins loose in her hands, looking down at the harbour, and did not turn round.
'I'll go down,' Wren said.

She gave Ash the reins and got off, and her legs were stiff enough that the first steps were a stagger. She walked down the track with the case under her arm. The case had grown to be part of her; she was aware of its weight the way she was aware of her own ribs. The gorse gave way to the last of the cultivated ground and then to the backs of the town, the net lofts and the fish sheds and the tar barrels, and she came in by the shore road, which was the road the men had run off along that night.

Nobody stopped her. A woman with a creel looked at her and looked away. A boy was mending a net on a wall and did not lift his head. She went up the lane between the houses and stood in the gap where the door had been.

The door itself was gone. The frame was charred back to black bone and someone had pulled the fallen timbers into a heap and left them, and the heap had been rained on until it was a mound of grey and black, like a barrow for something small. The survey room was under it. She stood and looked at the place where the table had been, and she could not find it. The floor was gone, the joists were gone, the window was a hole with the sea behind it, and where the window had been she could see, through the ruin, straight out to the water, which she could never do from the door before.
She had known it would be like this. She had seen the roof go. Knowing a thing and standing in it were two different trades.

She stepped in over the threshold. Ash had not come down with her, and Bryn had stayed on the box, and she was alone in the ruin, and the ash was soft under her boots, fine and grey and wet at the bottom. The smell of it was still there, thin and old, under the salt. She crouched and put her hand flat on the floorboards that were left at the edge of the room, and they were damp and cold and had gone soft with rot already.

Here was where the chair had stood. She could tell it by the scorch on the boards, a dark ring where the wing of it had burned down against the floor, and there was a shape in the ash inside the ring. She did not touch it. She did not know what it was and she did not want to. She stayed crouched a while with her hand on the cold board and her burned arm hanging, and the marks of Edric's cuff showed pale red on her wrist where the sleeve had ridden up, and she looked at them and then she looked away.

He had kept his door shut against the salt. Forty years of standing on wet ground and he had kept the door shut and the work exact, and they had come in after midnight and put the whole of it on the fire in a quarter of an hour, and the only thing that had come out of the house was the thing she had carried out, and the thing she had carried out was the reason they had come.

She got up and walked the length of the room. At the far end, under the fallen beam, she could see the corner of the chimney breast, and the brick was still there, the one loose brick that had hidden the seal tin, and it was half out of the wall and blackened but not fallen. She knelt and set the case down and worked the brick free with her fingers. Behind it the gap was empty and full of ash, and she sat back on her heels.

There was nothing here to find. There was nothing here at all. She had come down the hill to stand in a hole in a row of houses and there was nothing in it but ash and the sea coming through where the window used to be.
She heard him before she saw him, the crunch of his boots on the lane. He stopped in the doorway. She did not turn round.
'You'll want a minute,' Ash said.
'I've had it.'

He came in anyway and stood at the edge of the ash with his hat in his hands and his thin pink scar catching the light, and he looked round the ruin the way a man looks at a beast he's been asked to price. He had the money from the herd in his coat and his collar was still dark with his own blood from the wood, and he had come down the hill after her because he was the sort of man who would.
'They pulled the timbers out,' he said. 'Somebody's been at it. Neighbours, most like. You don't leave a fire like that to the wind in a town.'
'It doesn't matter,' Wren said.
'No.'

She stood in the middle of the room and turned round once, slowly, taking the whole of it in. The gable ends had held. The chimney had held. Everything else was gone, and the survey of Carrow Fell was in the case at her feet, and the seal was in the case, and the field books were in the case, and the only living person who could swear to any of it was standing in the ash with a burned arm and fourpence in her pocket.

Her face did something she had not given it leave to do. She put her hand up to stop it and it came anyway, and she stood there in the middle of Edric's house with her hand over her mouth and cried, and it was not a tidy thing and she did not try to make it one. Ash did not move to her and did not say anything, which was the right thing, and after a while the worst of it was past and she wiped her face on her sleeve, the good one, and blew out her breath.

'Six years,' she said. 'He taught me levels and boundaries and the run of the water and he never once said a kind thing to me that wasn't true. I sold his watch. That's the last of it. I sold my grandfather's watch and I gave my compass to a woman on a bridge and I've got fourpence and a dead man's survey and I'm standing in his kitchen.'
'It's his house,' Ash said. 'You can stand in it.'
'It's not a house. It's a hole.'
'It's his house,' he said again, and she let it be.

She picked up the case and went out past him into the lane, and the light off the water was very bright after the ruin and she stood a moment with her eyes shut. Down at the harbour a boat was coming in and men were calling to each other over the wall. Above her the gulls went round and round the chimney that was left, the way they had always done, because it was still the highest thing in the row and they did not know any different.

Ash came out and put his hat on. 'Bryn's waiting,' he said. 'And there's a man at the Drover's Rest in Harrowgate who knows your name, and there's a ferry below this town with an old man on it who'll ask you where you're going, and there's a road south from there. Thirteen days.'
'I know.'
'You'll want to be up on the hill before dark. She won't drive the cart by night on the moor.'

'No,' Wren said. She looked once more at the black gap in the row, and then she turned her back on it and started up the lane with the case under her arm, and Ash walked beside her, and neither of them said anything at all.

scenes.title: The shepherd's hut

beats: A storm drives them into a shepherd’s hut on Linmouth Moor, soaked to the skin.
They light a fire, eat what they have, and dry out as best they can.
Late into the night, Ash tells the story of how he became a drover, and Bryn tells a darker one about her father.
Wren cannot sleep and sits by the fire going over Edric’s survey, thinking about what it will mean.
card.mood: Storm outside, warmth inside, long talk.

paragraphs: They made the hill before the weather turned, but only just. The first spatter came off the sea as they came up through the gorse, big single drops that struck the back of Wren's neck like thrown gravel, and by the time Bryn had the cart turned off the track onto the moor path the whole sky had come down on them at once.

The wind came first, then the rain behind it, and it was not rain so much as the sea lifted up and carried inland. It drove flat across the moor with nothing to stop it. Wren put her head down and rode with her hand on the case and the water running off her chin into her collar. Cinder put his ears back and went on because there was nothing else to do.
'There,' Ash shouted, and pointed.

She could not see past the rain at first. Then the shape resolved out of it — a low stone hut with a turf roof, set against a bank where the ground folded over itself, so that from the west it was nothing but a hump of grass.
Bryn had already turned the cart towards it. Wren kicked Cinder after her.
The door was a plank on a leather hinge with a stone to hold it shut. Ash got it open and Bryn drove the cart into the lee of the bank behind the hut and set the brake before she came in.

Inside it was dark and smelled of old smoke and sheep. The floor was beaten earth with a flat stone in the middle for a hearth, and there was a low bench along one wall, and a bed of heather and bracken in the corner that had gone grey and dry. The roof was sound. The rain hammered on the turf above them and did not come through.

Wren got the case down and set it on the bench, and then she got her oilskin off, which took a while, because the wet had made the buttons stubborn and her left hand did not want to close properly. She hung it on the peg beside the door. She sat down on the bench and pulled off her boots, and the water came out of them, and she set them on their sides near the hearth with the toes towards the fire they had not lit yet. Her feet were white and wrinkled and she did not put anything on them.

There was a box under the bench, and in the box a shirt. Grey wool, worn soft, gone thin at the elbows, with a smell to it of woodsmoke and sheep and something older underneath. She looked at it a while.
'It's dry,' Ash said. 'That's all I ask of a house.'

She turned her back and got out of the jumper with the melted sleeve and the torn hem, and got the shirt on over her bandage, and it came down to the top of her thighs and the sleeves hung past her hands. Then she sat down by the hearth with her feet out towards the fire she was going to build, and she was barefoot and out of her coat for the first time in seventeen days.

Bryn had the fire going before Wren had finished with the shirt. She carried dry kindling in the cart, because she had carted twenty years, and she had turf blocks too, and a handful of small coal wrapped in sacking, and in a little while the flat stone in the middle of the floor was hot and the hut had gone from cold and dark to something else entirely.

They ate what they had. Bread gone hard, a lump of cheese, three cold potatoes between them from a pot Bryn had boiled two nights back, and a strip of the bacon that was left, which Wren counted in her head and decided was four days' worth if they were careful and two if they were not. The rain came on the roof. The wind came round the gable and found the crack above the door and made a noise in it like someone breathing.

Nobody said much. Ash got his coat off and hung it over the bench and sat with his back to the wall with his boots off and his socks steaming. Bryn filled her pipe from a twist of cloth and smoked it and watched the door, the way she watched everything, without hurry.

Wren unwound her bandage and looked at the arm in the firelight. The blisters had gone down at the wrist. The red flower of Edric's cuff was still there on the flesh, paler than it had been, but there. She greased it from the pot and wound the linen back on, one-handed, and Bryn watched her do it and did not offer to help, which Wren was glad of.
'Weather like this,' Ash said, 'you can't do anything with it. You can't ride it out and you can't walk it off. You've got to sit and let it rain.'
'You'd know,' Bryn said.
'I've sat in this hut before. Two nights once, with a bull that wouldn't be led and a dog that wouldn't be called.'
'That'd be the bull you walked Harrowgate to Fallow Cross.'
'That'd be the one.'

Wren lay down on the heather with the case for a pillow and her feet to the fire and did not sleep. Ash told the story of the bull and the dog and the gate, and it was a good story and he told it well, and she lay with her eyes shut and listened to the roof.

He had been fifteen when he started on the road, he said. His father had a few acres above Drake's Bottom and no use for him and less for his mouth, and there had been a man coming through the village with six head and a boy wanted, and Ash had gone out of the door with what he stood in and never gone back to live. He had learned droving the way a dog learns sheep, from being wrong at it often enough in front of people who would not let him forget it. The first winter he had lost two beasts in a snowdrift and been docked for them, and he had cried about it in a barn, and the man he worked for had found him at it and said nothing, and the next morning had shown him how to read a sky. He had been on the road fifteen years since and could not sleep in a bed under a roof without waking at four.
Wren had heard some of it before, on the drove road, in pieces. She had not heard the part about the barn.
'Fifteen,' Bryn said. 'You were all knees and opinions.'
'I was all knees and opinions and I was right about most of it.'

'You were wrong about the fire,' Bryn said, and it was not a question, and Ash did not answer it, and after a moment she went on herself, and her voice was the same flat voice she used for the price of a shoe.

Her father had been a farrier in Harrowgate with a yard behind the house and a hand gone bad at the wrist, and he had drunk, and when he drank he was a man who wanted a reason. Bryn had been the reason often enough. The scar on the back of her hand was not from any forge, and she said so, and turned the hand over in the firelight so that Wren could see the white shape of it, and then put it back in her lap.

The strong arm of the family had gone to his wife's people at Carrow twelve years back, she said. She had not seen him since and did not want the Warden's men carrying her name down that road before her.
That was all she said about it. No more than that, and nothing to follow it, and Ash did not try to fill the gap, which Wren noticed.

Wren lay with her eyes on the roof beams and did not sleep. The others did. Ash went over first, with his mouth open and his hand on his knife the way he slept, and then Bryn, who lay down on the bench with her boots under her head and her whip beside her, which was how she slept, and in a while the two of them were breathing slow and even and the fire had burned down to a red bed on the flat stone.
Wren got up. She took the case off the bench and sat down by the fire with it across her knees and opened the flap.

The maps were in the first fold, rolled and wrapped in oiled cloth. She unrolled the top sheet on the stone and weighted the corners with the coal lump and a turf block and looked at Carrow Fell in Edric's hand. The contour lines, drawn at ten-foot intervals, close together on the north side where the ground went up over the old workings. The beck running down from the moss. The Crown grant boundary marked in red, which Edric had drawn in the office at Linmouth from the deed, and then the levels in black, which he had walked and chained and levelled himself over six weeks of a bad spring, and which ran a mile and a half past the red line and stopped.

There. At the end of the black line, in the corner of the sheet, he had written the date and his initials, and below that, in smaller letters, the depth of the adit mouth below the surface, and the run of the water, and the word *silver* once, underlined, and no more.

He had been sixty-eight and his knees were gone and he had gone up that fell six weeks in the wet to walk a level he could already have guessed at, because a survey that is not walked is not a survey, and he had known he was dying.
She looked at the black line a long time.

If it went on the record, the levels were open. Anyone could work them and the grant could not be sworn over them, because the record would stand, and the record would stand because she would have carried it there and sworn it in his name and hers. That was what it would mean. Vey would lose the fell and the town below it would not be sold out from under it, and the men who had come in the night and the man who had stood in the ford and the man with the book at the bridge and the twenty crowns in gold would all of them have spent their time for nothing.

And if she did not get there, it was a year, and in a year there would be no survey and no Edric and no old man in a chair by a window and the fell would be Vey's and the levels would be a story told by a girl with a burned arm in a shepherd's hut on the moor.

She folded the map and put it back in the oiled cloth and put the cloth back in the case. She put the case on the bench and sat down again with her feet on the warm stone, and outside the rain went on and on across the whole moor with nothing in its way, and inside the hut it was warm.

She thought about the last thing he had said to her, which had not been kind. It had been about the chain, and the second chain, and the allowance for the sag in the line, and he had said it in the doorway with his coat on and she had not known it was the last thing. He had never once said a kind thing to her that was not true.

She was going to get there. It was fourteen days, and then thirteen, and now it was twelve, and she was barefoot in a dead shepherd's shirt with fourpence in her pocket, and she was going to get there, and it was not a hope, it was an account, and the account balanced.
The fire settled. The wind found the crack above the door again and breathed in it. Somewhere out on the moor, a long way off, something moved that was probably a sheep.

Wren leaned back against the bench and put her feet out to the red of the fire and stayed awake, and the storm went on over the hut, and she sat with the case at her shoulder and waited for the morning.

scenes.title: Down to the river

beats: The storm has passed; they come down off the moor towards the Linn.
Bryn worries the river is too high for the ferry; Ash makes jokes.
From the last hill they see the ferry landing and smoke from Oskar’s chimney.

paragraphs: Wren heard the change before she saw it. The rain on the turf roof slackened from a drumming to a patter, then to single drops shaken loose by the wind, and then to nothing. The wind itself went round to the north and came clean and cold under the door, and the fire on the hearth stone had burned down to a red bed with grey on it, and she had sat through the whole night without lying down.

She stood, and her feet woke up in pins and needles against the cold flag of the floor. Her boots had dried stiff by the hearth. She worked them on, and the left one went on over the bandage with a bit of a shove.

Ash was asleep sitting up with his back to the wall, his mouth open, one hand loose on the knife at his belt. Bryn lay along the bench with her boots under her head and her whip beside her, and she was not asleep. Wren knew it before she moved, from the way she was breathing.
‘It’s stopped,’ Wren said.

‘It’s stopped here,’ Bryn said, without opening her eyes. ‘It’ll have rained all night on the top of everything that runs to the Linn. Every beck and gill between here and the ferry is carrying it down to the same place.’

Wren went out. The morning was white and cold and the whole moor stood in it, every stone washed and every rush standing up straight and dripping. The bank behind the hut had run with water in the night and cut a little channel through the turf by the corner, and Cinder stood in the lee of it with his head down and his back to the wind, the cart tilted where a wheel had settled into the soft ground.

The sea was out there somewhere to the west, hidden under the white. Below them, in the folds, the ground fell away towards the valley of the Linn, and somewhere down in that whiteness was the river, and the ferry, and the two coppers she had promised Oskar Venn three weeks ago.

‘The road down,’ Bryn said behind her. She had her leather apron on over her wet coat and her pipe unlit between her teeth. ‘It’ll be a slough by now. We’ll be to the bottom by middle day if we take it slow and I don’t ask the horse for anything clever.’
‘And the ferry?’

‘That’s what I’m telling you.’ Bryn looked down the valley, and there was nothing on her face either way. ‘A river that size, after a night like that one, comes up three foot by morning and another foot by noon. Venn’s cable will be under water. He’ll not run it if he can’t see his landing on the far side.’
Ash came out of the hut with his coat half on, his hair flat on one side, blinking at the light like a man who had been woken by a bucket. He looked at the sky. He looked at the valley.
‘It’s a fine morning,’ he said.
‘It’s a flood,’ Bryn said.

‘It’s a fine morning and a flood, and they’re not the same thing, cousin.’ He got his other arm into the coat. ‘I’ve crossed that water when it was up over the landing stage and Venn took us over sitting down, eating an apple, and never said a word about it. He’s a ferryman. That’s what a ferryman is for. If he only ran it when the water was pretty he’d starve.’
‘He’d drown and then starve,’ Bryn said. ‘In that order, and be no use to the girl either way. Get the horse.’

They got the horse. Cinder took the collar and stood while they put the shafts to rights, and Bryn walked him down off the bank with the cart braking behind him, and the wheel that had settled in the soft ground came out with a sucking noise and a shake. Then the road, such as it was, went down by the wall and the old sheep fold and turned along the side of the valley, and the whole of it was running water, brown and quick, cutting little gullies through the gravel where it went.

Wren walked in front with the case across her chest. The ground had a skin on it that held for the first step and gave on the second, and by the time they had gone a mile her boots weighed twice what they had, and the hem of the dead shepherd’s shirt was black to the knee. Ash walked at the tail of the cart with his collar up and his hands in his armpits and his mouth shut, which for Ash was a kind of weather in itself.

They heard the river before they saw it. It came up the valley as a steady sound, not a roar but something wide, like a crowd a long way off, and the white air thinned as they came down and the far side of the valley came through it, first the shape of the hill and then the wood on it, grey and brown, and then the water.

Wren stopped on the last rise and looked at it. The Linn was twice the width it had been the morning she had come up this way on foot, and it was not brown, it was a pale clay colour, and it was moving. Whole trees came down it, turning slowly. Where the ferry landing had been there was water and a bit of the stone wall standing out of it, and the punt lay hauled up the bank on the far side, high, with the cable run out and sagging into the flood. And over on the east bank, above the landing, there was a thread of blue smoke going up straight from the chimney of the ferryman’s house, standing in the still cold air like a line ruled on paper.
‘There,’ Wren said. ‘He’s there. He’s not gone anywhere.’
Bryn stood beside her with the reins in her hand and looked at the water a while, and looked at the smoke, and looked at the water again.
‘He’s there,’ she said. ‘That’s his chimney. That doesn’t say he’ll put that punt on that river today for two coppers and a girl with a case. Look at it. It’s got the whole moor in it.’

‘He’ll have to put it on for something,’ Ash said. He came up and stood at Wren’s shoulder and looked down at the flood with his head on one side, and the thin pink line under his eye went tight with the cold. ‘There’s a girl down there he’s fond of. He’ll not sit by his fire a week while the town starves behind a river. He’ll run it by tomorrow, and if he runs it by tomorrow there’s no reason on God’s earth why he can’t run it today for the right person, and the right person is standing here in a dead man’s shirt with a survey on her back and two coppers in her pocket, which is exactly the sort of person a ferryman likes, because he’s one himself.’
‘You’ve got fourpence,’ Bryn said.

‘Fourpence,’ Wren said. ‘Two for him and two for her. That was the price before and it’ll be the price now, and if it isn’t the price now then I’ll find out what the price is and pay it.’ She looked down at the water. ‘There’s no other way over. Not today. Not for forty miles either side, unless there’s a bridge I don’t know about, and I know about the bridges.’

Bryn spat into the flood below the wall and wiped her mouth with the back of her scarred hand. ‘Then we go down and ask him,’ she said, ‘and if he says no, we sit on the bank and wait till he says yes, and if he never says yes, I’ll take you back up to the salt road by the south and it’ll cost you four days you don’t have. Get in the cart. The last bit’s the worst.’

Wren climbed up beside the boxes with the case against her knees. Ash took Cinder’s halter and led him behind, and Bryn walked the horse down the last of the hill with her weight against the shafts and her boots skidding in the wet, and the sound of the river got up under all of it, wide and steady and going somewhere with no hurry at all.

scenes.title: The crossing

beats: At the landing Oskar says the river is too high, then agrees to take them across for double fare.
The crossing is hard; the cart and horses go over in two trips while Oskar and Bryn haul on the rope.
On the far bank Pell is waiting at the landing, and they say their goodbyes to her before riding on.

paragraphs: The landing was gone. Where the stone flags had been there was a grey swirl and the top of the wall, and the bank itself cut away in a raw lip of clay that went down into the water and did not come up again. The punt lay hauled out on the far side, tilted up the bank with its bow in the alders, and the cable ran from it across the flood and down into the water and came up again at the near-side post, sagging in a long curve with the current pulling at it, and the post itself stood in two feet of moving water.
Bryn brought the cart round and set the brake and got down, and stood looking at the post. Ash led Cinder up beside the tailgate and stood with his hand on the halter and said nothing.

The ferryman's door opened on the far bank. Oskar Venn came out with a rope over his shoulder and stood on his own landing looking across at them, and he did not wave and did not shout. He came down the bank and got into the punt with his weight on the cable, and he worked the punt out into the flood hand over hand, and the water took it downstream and he hauled it back and the punt came across the river sideways and slow and low, shipping grey water over the near gunwale, and it took him a long time.
He brought it in below the landing where the bank still held, and stood in it with the rope in his fist and looked at the three of them and the cart and the two horses.
'Not today,' he said.
'You're here,' Wren said.

'I'm here. That's not the river.' He nodded at the water. 'She's up three foot on yesterday and still coming. I can't see my landing on the far side from the middle. When I can't see my landing I don't go, and I've not gone these thirty years and I've not drowned either.'
'I can see it,' Wren said. 'It's behind you.'
'Aye,' Oskar said. 'And I'd be looking at it from the middle with the whole moor coming at me sideways. You'll wait. She'll drop by tomorrow and the day after she'll be fit.'
'I can't wait.'
'Then you'll walk,' Oskar said, 'and you'll not walk, because there's no bridge.'

Wren climbed down out of the cart and stood on the wet clay at the edge and looked at him. He was an old man with grey stubble and a broken front tooth and flat pale eyes, and he stood in the punt with the rope across his shoulder and the water running past him, and he was not being cruel. He was doing the sum.

'I've got fourpence,' she said. 'The price was two coppers for me and two for the horse. There's three of us and two horses and a cart and a load. I'll pay double what the four of us come to. I'll pay it now, and if the punt goes over I'll not blame you and there's nobody to blame you anyway, because there's no one on this bank but us.'
'Double,' Oskar said.
'Double.'

He looked at the cart a while. He looked at Bryn, and at the leather apron and the scarred hand and the pipe. He looked at Ash and the thin pink line under his eye, and at Cinder standing with his head down and his back to the wind. Then he looked at Wren, at the sleeves hanging past her hands and the case on her back and the way she stood with her weight off the left arm.
'You're the girl that came up this way in the spring,' he said. 'With the burned arm and the surveyor's case and the bead you owe my Pell.'
'That's me.'
'She's had that bead off you every day since. She's told the whole town you're coming back with it.'
'I've got it,' Wren said. 'It's in my jumper.'

Oskar stood in the punt and looked at the river for a while longer, and then he spat into it and said, 'Get the horse out and put the cart on first. The horses after. Two trips. And you'll stand in the middle and not move about, and if you go in I'll not go after you, because I can't swim and I'll not drown for a stranger.' He looked at her again. 'Which you're not, now.'

Bryn had already backed the horse and was unhitching. She did it fast, the way she did everything, and Wren held the shaft while the horse came out, and Ash took the horse up the bank out of the way. Then they rolled the cart down the slip and onto the punt by hand, Bryn at the near wheel and Oskar in the punt with his shoulder against the shaft, and the punt went down under the weight until the water came over the gunwale and then steadied, and the horse was led on and stood trembling with its head up and its ears back.
'Get on,' Oskar said.

Bryn got on and took the horse's head. Wren stayed where she was. The punt went out into the flood with Oskar hauling on the cable and Bryn hauling with him, both of them bent to it and the rope creaking, and the punt went downstream at once and had to be walked back up against the current, and the water came over the side in little waves and ran out through the boards. Halfway across the cable went under and Oskar had to feel for it with his hands, up to the elbows, and the punt swung and the horse scrabbled and Bryn put her weight on its head and talked to it flat and steady, and then the cable came up again and they hauled the last of it and the punt grounded on the far bank and Bryn walked the horse off up onto the grass and came back for the boxes.
Then the punt went back across empty, and it was harder going back, and Oskar came in below the landing with his chest heaving and his coat black with water, and did not say anything about it.
'Now the horses,' he said.

Cinder went on badly. He put his foot on the boards and took it off again twice, and Ash had to get in front of him and lead him, and once he was on he stood with his legs braced wide and his eyes rolling at the water, and Wren got on behind him and put her hand flat on his neck and kept it there. Ash stood in the middle of the punt with his feet apart and his hands in his armpits, and said, 'If he goes, I go, and I'll not hear the end of it.'
'You'll not go,' Bryn said from the far bank.

The second crossing was worse than the first. The cable was under for twenty yards of it and Oskar took them through by the feel of it in his hands, and the punt turned twice and came round again, and water came in over the bow and Ash bailed with his hat. Wren watched the far bank the whole way, the alder roots and the raw bank and the smoke going up straight from the chimney, and she did not look at the water, and then Cinder's hooves were on the boards of the landing and the boards were on stone and they were across.

Pell was waiting at the top of the bank. She had a coat on and no shoes, and her plaits were coming undone, and she stood there with her hands behind her back, watching, and when Wren had led Cinder up onto the grass she came down two steps and stopped.
'You came back,' she said.
'I said I would.'
'You said however long it took.'
'It took a while,' Wren said.

She got the bead out of her jumper pocket. It was a blue glass bead the size of a hazelnut, with a white thread running through it, and it had been in her pocket through the rain at the ford and the night in the hut and it was still whole. She put it in Pell's hand.
Pell looked at it for a long moment and did not say anything, and then she closed her fingers round it and turned and ran up the bank to the house and was gone, and they heard the door.

'She'll be back,' Oskar said. He had the rope coiled over his shoulder and he was standing in the wet coat with the water running off the hem of it. 'She'll want to show it to her aunt and then she'll be back.'

They loaded the cart and hitched the horse and Bryn made the harness fast and got up. Ash took Cinder's halter. Wren stood by the tailgate with the case against her hip and looked back across the river at the west bank, the whole of it, the clay lip and the sunken wall and the road they had come down, and there was nothing on it. No horse, no man, no grey coat. The river went past under the cable and the cable hung over it, dripping.
Pell came back down the bank with her fist closed and stood beside her father and opened her hand and looked at the bead again, and closed it.
'It's got a white thread in it,' she said.
'I know,' Wren said.
'Where does the thread go?'
'Right through,' Wren said. 'It's the same the whole way. That's how they make them.'
Pell turned it over in her palm. Then she looked up at Wren, at the case and the sleeve pulled down over the bandage, and said, 'Are you coming back this way?'
'Not this way,' Wren said.
'Then I'll keep it,' Pell said, and put it in her coat pocket and closed the flap over it, and stood with her hand flat on the flap, as though she had put it away somewhere and meant it to stay.

Oskar walked round to the back of the cart and put his hand on the tailgate and looked up at Bryn. 'You'll make the salt road by dark if you push,' he said. 'Road's a slough past the second beck. There's a stone barn at the top of the rise, the roof's half on. If it rains again you'll want it.'
'It'll not rain,' Bryn said.
'It'll rain Thursday,' Oskar said.
Bryn clicked the horse and the cart moved off up the track, and Ash went after it with Cinder, and Wren stood a moment longer with the case in her hand.
'You'll not get the double fare back,' Oskar said. 'I've spent it.'
'It's not for getting back,' Wren said.

She went up the track after the cart. At the top of the rise she looked back once, and the ferry landing was small below her, and the punt was out in the middle of the flood already, going back, with the old man in it and the girl sitting in the stern with her coat round her and her hand in her pocket, and the smoke going up straight from the chimney behind them, and then the cart went over the rise and she could not see it any more.

scenes.title: The Wheatsheaf

beats: They reach Carrow and take rooms at the Wheatsheaf on the market square.
The landlord tells them the Assize sits the day after tomorrow, and that the Warden’s man has been asking about a survey.
Over a long supper by the fire Ash and Wren talk about what they will do after Carrow, and whether he will stay.
Wren goes over the survey one last time while Ash dozes in his chair.

paragraphs: They came into Carrow in the last of the light, down the long straight of the salt road that ran between the fell on the left and the flat green land on the right, and the town came up out of the ground slowly the way market towns do, first the abbey tower and then the roofs and then the whole grey mass of it smoking into a sky the colour of pewter. Wren had been two days on the road since the ferry, and she had stopped counting the miles somewhere past the second beck and started counting the hours instead.

The streets were narrow and full of carts. Cinder put his head down and went through the crowd like a man going home. Ash had ridden him the last four miles, since Wren's arm had started up again after the wet, and she had walked with the case against her hip and her boots squelching.

The Wheatsheaf stood on the market square with its back to the abbey and its sign swinging on a bracket over the door, a bundle of wheat painted on it gone brown with weather. The square was laid out with posts and rails for the cattle market, empty now, and a pump at the corner with three women round it and a boy filling a yoke of buckets. Bryn pulled the cart up at the door and sat looking at it a while before she got down.
‘We'll want a room,’ she said.
‘Room's for two,’ said Wren.
‘There's three of us.’
‘There's two of us that need beds. I'll sleep in the cart.’

‘You'll not sleep in the cart, and I'll not have you say I put you there.’ Bryn got down off the seat and stood on the cobbles with her hands on her hips, reading the sign the way she read everything, without hurry. ‘Two rooms, and I'll take the second and put my own money down for it, and you'll not argue about that in the street.’
Wren did not argue.

The landlord was a short, bald man called Rafe with a cloth over his shoulder and flour on his hands, and he came out wiping them and looked at the three of them and the cart and the horses and counted it all up in about four seconds.
‘Two rooms,’ he said. ‘Top of the stair. Market side, fourpence the night, back side, threepence. Which?’
‘Market side,’ said Bryn.

‘There's a good fire in the common room and there's supper on at six and the Assize is the day after tomorrow, so you'll be paying the Assize price,’ he said, and said it as a fact rather than an apology, ‘and I'll want the horses put up at the Crown, because I've no stalls, I've only the yard.’
‘The horses are going to the farrier,’ said Bryn. ‘Where's the smith?’
‘Far end of the square, past the cross, the one with the white door.’

Bryn had the harness off and the boxes down and Cinder's saddle off inside ten minutes, and then she took both horses on a lead rein and walked away down the square with the light going and her apron flapping at her knees, and Wren stood in the doorway of the Wheatsheaf with the case in her hand and watched her go.

‘She'll not be back before morning,’ said Ash, coming up behind her with his hat in his hand. ‘That one'll stand and watch a smith for an hour and tell him the whole of his trade wrong, and then she'll want a drink with him, and then she'll find somebody who knows somebody from Harrowgate, and then it'll be morning.’
‘She'll come back,’ Wren said.

‘She'll come back. I said before morning, not never.’ He went in past her, and then stopped in the doorway and stood there with his hand on the frame, looking at the room, and let out a long breath through his nose. ‘That'll do,’ he said. ‘That'll do very well.’

The common room of the Wheatsheaf was low and long and dark at the beams, and there was a fire in the middle of it on a stone hearth, and a settle on either side, and a table with a bench, and three men at the far end playing cards with their caps on. The smoke went up and lay along the ceiling. It smelled of woodsmoke and old beer and bread, and under it the wet wool of everyone who had come in out of the day. Wren thought that if she had been asked to draw the room she would have got the fire wrong and the beams wrong and everything else right.
Rafe brought them a jug and two cups and stood over them while they drank, and it was clear he had been waiting to say something since they came in.
‘You'll have come for the Assize,’ he said.
‘We'll have come for the town,’ said Ash.

‘Everyone's come for the Assize. It's been sitting three days and it sits the day after tomorrow and it rises when it's done, and there's wool men and fell men and a lawyer from the south in the room over the door.’ He leaned his elbow on the settle end. ‘You'll want to know the other thing, though. There's been a man in here asking about a survey.’
Wren had the cup halfway to her mouth. She put it down without hurrying, which took more out of her than the cup had.
‘A survey,’ she said.

‘Aye. Grey coat, no mud on him. Monday, and again yesterday. Asking had anyone come in with a survey, had anyone come in with a case, had anyone come in off the salt road. I told him no, and I'll tell you the same, because it's true.’ Rafe scratched under his chin. ‘He's been to the abbey as well, and the assay, and the man at the Crown. He pays for his drink and he pays for other people's, and he asks his questions quiet, but he's asked them of every door in this town, and there's not a landlord in Carrow who doesn't know what he's after by now.’
‘And what's he after?’ Ash said.

‘A survey,’ said Rafe, with the patience of a man who has answered the question already. ‘I've told you all I know.’ He wiped the table with his cloth, though the table was clean, and went away to the card players.

Wren sat with her hands round her cup. Ash was looking at her; she could feel it, and she didn't look back at him, not yet. Two days to the Assize. The man was here. He had been here since Monday, and this was the twentieth, and he had asked at every door, which meant he was not hiding, which meant he did not have to.
‘He doesn't know what it is,’ she said at last, quietly. ‘If he knew, he'd not be asking the doors. He'd be at the abbey with a lawyer.’
‘He's not asking the doors for his own sake,’ said Ash. ‘He knows what it is. He's just not the one who wants it. He's the hand.’
Wren turned her cup a quarter-turn on the table.
‘Then the hand's been in Carrow since Monday,’ she said.

They ate at the table by the fire with their backs to the room, which was the way Ash had put it, and the food came out of the kitchen in a procession: a mutton broth, then a pie with a crust on it like a roof, then a plate of bacon and greens, then a cheese, then a bowl of apples stewed with honey, and Rafe brought a second jug without being asked and stood it on the table and went away. Wren ate as though the plate might be taken from her, because for two days on the road it had been bread and cheese and a handful of oats boiled in a pot, and because there had been a time on the towpath when she had gone a day and a night on nothing, and her body had not forgotten it.

Ash ate more slowly. He had come in from the road with his collar up and his hands in his armpits and had said almost nothing all afternoon, and now the fire had got into him and the colour was coming back into his face and the thin pink line under his eye had gone soft at the edges, the way a scar does when a man has been warm for an hour.
‘You'll go up to the abbey in the morning,’ he said.
‘The day after tomorrow. It's laid on the day, not before.’

‘You'll go up in the morning and look at the door of it, then. Know which way it opens.’ He tore a piece of bread. ‘I'd go with you, but I'll be at the Crown all morning seeing if there's a herd going north. There's a man there with forty head of Galloway and no drover, and he's been asking.’
Wren put her knife down.
‘Going north,’ she said.

‘Going north is where the work is.’ He said it lightly, the way he said most things, but he had turned his cup round so the handle faced him, and he was looking at the cup and not at her. ‘There's Ashbourne market in ten days and the road up past the Drover's Rest, and I know every field and every nighting place the whole of the way, and a man with forty head of Galloway needs somebody who knows the road, and I know the road.’
‘You could go south with me,’ Wren said. ‘There's land south. There's work south.’

‘There's work everywhere there's beasts.’ He grinned at her, and the grin was the one he used for horse dealers and gatekeepers, and she had seen him use it often enough to know it. ‘I'm not saying I'll go north. I'm saying I'll be at the Crown in the morning and I'll hear what the man says, which is a different thing, and if he says a word I don't like I'll walk out of the door and come back here and have dinner, and then you'll know.’
‘That's not an answer.’
‘No,’ he said. ‘It's not.’ He drank. ‘What'll you do? After. When it's on the record and the seal's broke and the whole town's read it in the abbey book.’
Wren thought about it properly, because he had asked properly, and because she had been turning it over herself every night since the hut on the moor and had not got to the end of it.

‘There's Thistle at the farm,’ she said. ‘Two shillings for the fortnight, and that's near a month now, and Hobb's wife will have it in her head that I'm not coming, so that's the first thing. Then I'll go up to the fell and walk the levels myself, the way he would have done. The survey's his and it goes in his name and mine, and after that it's on the record and anyone can read it, and there's no more to be done with it, but somebody has to walk it. There's a drain above the second beck he was never sure of. He wrote it in the margin and he never got up there again.’ She stopped. ‘That's not an answer either. That's just the next thing.’
‘It's an answer,’ Ash said. ‘It's just a drover's answer. You do the next thing and the next thing, and if the ground holds you keep going.’
‘And if it doesn't?’
‘Then you stand still and let it dry.’ He pushed the bowl of apples towards her. ‘Eat those. Rafe's charging for them whether we eat them or not, and I've a mind to get the value.’

The fire burned down. The card players went out one by one, and Rafe banked the far end of the hearth and put the shutters to and went up, and the room was left to the two of them and the red light and the tick of the settle as the wood cooled. Wren had the case on the bench beside her, where it had been all evening, and she pulled it onto her knees and unbuckled it.
Ash had his boots off and his feet to the fire and his hat over his face, and he was not asleep, but he was doing a good impression of it.
‘You'll not read the whole of it again,’ he said from under the hat.
‘I'll read the last page.’
‘You've read the last page forty times.’

‘Then this'll be forty-one.’ She got the field book out and laid it flat on the case with the lamp pulled near, and turned to the back, where the levels ran down the page in Edric's small tight hand, every figure ruled and every figure checked and the last line of it running a mile and a half past the beck and past the boundary of the Crown grant, and under it, alone on the page, the word he had written and gone over twice so the ink stood up off the paper: *silver*.

She read it the way she had read it every night. She read the figures and did the sums in her head and got the same answers, and she read the note in the margin about the drain, and she looked at the signature block at the foot of the page, which was blank, waiting for two names, and at the seal in the tin at the bottom of the case, brass and cold, and she thought about the clerk at the assay office in Harrowgate who had stopped his pen when she said Edric Rone, and about Rafe's grey-coated man who had asked at every door in Carrow since Monday, and about the day after tomorrow.

Ash was properly asleep now, his mouth a little open, his hat slid down over his nose, one hand hanging off the end of the settle. His boots stood by the hearth with the wet dried out of them. He had said he would be at the Crown in the morning and would hear what the man said and would come back and have his dinner, and she did not know whether he would go north or stay, and neither did he, and that was the truth of it and she would not make it into anything else.

Wren closed the field book and put it in the case and buckled the strap, and slid the case under the bench and put her foot against it. The fire was down to embers. Somewhere past the shutters the abbey bell rang the hour, slow and flat, and she counted it without meaning to, the way she counted everything, and then she sat in the dark by the dying fire with her burned arm across her knees and waited for the morning.

scenes.title: Fog on the fell

beats: Wren and Ash ride up Carrow Fell to see the old workings with their own eyes.
Fog comes down thick; they have to find the way to the north side by what they can see and remember of the survey.
They find the old adit, black and dripping, exactly where Edric drew it.

paragraphs: They were on the fell by seven, with the fog still lying in the hollows below them and the town gone to a grey smudge at the bottom of the world.

Ash had come back from the Crown at noon the day before with nothing worth the walking: the man with the Galloway had gone north on Tuesday, and the drover's place with him. He had eaten his dinner and said nothing about it, and Wren had said nothing either, and in the morning he had been standing in the yard with Cinder saddled before she came down. He had not said he was coming. He had simply held the stirrup.
‘You'll want a witness,’ he said, when she looked at him. ‘Surveys want witnesses. I've heard that said.’
‘A witness to what?’
‘To you standing on it.’ He swung up behind her. ‘I've nothing else to do until Thursday.’

The road up out of Carrow ran north between walls, and then the walls gave out and the ground began to climb in earnest, wet and tussocky, cut about with old peat spits, and the fell opened above them, brown and green and very large. Edric's map was in the case on Wren's back, but she had copied the run of it into her head weeks ago, and she did not need the paper for the first mile. The beck came down on their right, the second beck, and above it, on the shoulder of the hill, a scatter of grey stones that were not stones.
They were spoil. She had known they would be, from the survey. She had not known how much of it there would be.

The heaps ran along the hillside in a broken line, grown over with heather and whin, and among them the ground was pitted with hollows and the hollows were full of black water. Ash walked Cinder along the edge of it and stopped.
‘That's a lot of digging,’ he said.

‘Forty years of it. More. They worked it in the old queen's time and then the water came in.’ Wren was off the horse already, on her knees at the edge of the nearest pit, and the burned arm complained and she ignored it. She got a handful of the spoil and rubbed it between her fingers. Grey, fine, cold. ‘This is the wash. They broke it small and washed it here. There'll be a leat above us somewhere, and a pond.’
‘And the hole they went in at?’

‘The adit.’ She stood, wiping her hand on the dead shepherd's shirt. ‘North side, under the crag. Edric drew it at three hundred and forty feet above the beck mouth, bearing north by east from the second cairn. If the cairn's standing.’
‘If the fog lets you see it.’

She looked up. The fog had been a band across the middle of the fell when they started; now it was moving down on them, slow and level, the way fog moves on a hill, and the top of the fell had already gone into it. The cairn, wherever it was, was not there to be seen.
‘Then we go by the map,’ she said, and got the case down and opened it on a flat stone, and took out the survey.

They went on up. The fog came down over them in the next quarter hour, and after that there was no world at all beyond twenty yards: no town, no valley, no sky, only the wet brown ground and the spoil heaps coming up one after another out of the white and going away behind them. The wind had dropped. Water dripped off the whins. Cinder put his feet down carefully and blew through his nose, and Ash talked to him in a low voice and led him on.

Wren walked in front with the map, which was useless in the fog and she knew it was useless, and she used it anyway, because it was the only thing she had that was true. She counted her paces. She had paced it out in the survey room a hundred times in her head and she paced it now on the ground, and at four hundred she stopped and checked the bearing she had scratched into the margin and went on again, and the ground got steeper and rockier and the spoil gave out, and there was nothing but the white and the sound of her boots and the horse behind her.
‘You've a way of counting under your breath,’ Ash said.
‘It's the only way I know to keep the line.’
‘And if the line's wrong?’

‘Then we walk in a circle in the fog until it lifts.’ She stopped and looked back at him. It came to her that she could see him and no further, and that if she walked on ten paces she would not see him at all. ‘You could wait here with the horse. There's no sense in both of us being lost.’
‘I've been lost before,’ Ash said. ‘It's mostly dull.’

She went on. The ground rose, and the rock came up through it, and the fog was so thick now that she could put her hand out and feel the water standing on the air. She counted to two hundred more and then she stopped counting, because she had lost the count and could not remember whether it was two hundred or two hundred and forty, and she stood still in the middle of the white fell and felt the whole thing tilt under her: the survey, the days, the case on her back, the dead man's small tight hand. Edric had walked this. Edric had stood here with the chain and the theodolite and got it right. If she could not find a hole in the ground that he had found and drawn, then the rest of it was nothing.
‘Wren.’ Ash's voice, close. ‘You've stopped.’
‘I've lost the count.’
‘Then lose it and look at the ground.’ He came up beside her, leading Cinder, and pointed down. ‘What's that under your boot?’

She looked down. There was a line in the ground at her feet, a long shallow groove running away into the fog, grown in with heather and moss but still a groove, and beside it a low bank of earth and stone.

‘That's a leat,’ she said. Her voice came out flat and strange. ‘That's the leat. The water from the pond. It runs to the adit mouth and they turned it down the shaft to work the ground, and when they gave up they let it run in and flood the levels.’ She was on her knees with the map spread on the wet grass before she had finished the sentence. ‘The leat runs from the pond to the adit. It's on the survey. It's drawn to the chain. If we follow the leat down, it takes us to the mouth.’
‘Then follow the leat,’ Ash said.

They followed it. The groove deepened as they went, cut into the hillside, and the ground fell away on their left, and the fog thinned by a degree and then by more, because they had come round the shoulder of the hill out of the wind and into the lee of the crag, and there was a grey shape of rock above them that was the crag, and below it a darker grey that was not rock.

The leat ended in a channel cut into the rock face, and the channel went into a black mouth in the hillside, and the mouth was timbered, and the timbers were still there, black and sodden, holding up the roof of it, and water dripped off the ends of the timbers into a pool at the entrance and ran away down the hill in a thread of brown water.
Wren stood in front of it. She took the map out and held it up against the hillside, and the drawing on the paper and the hole in the ground lined up the way a key lines up with a lock.
‘That's it,’ she said. ‘That's the adit. North side of the fell, three hundred and forty feet above the beck mouth, bearing north by east from the second cairn. He drew it and it's there.’
Ash came up beside her. He took his hat off, which he did not do often, and looked into the black mouth, and the drips went on falling into the pool, one and then another and then another.
‘How far in does it go?’

‘A mile and a half past the beck, by his levels. That's the whole of it.’ She folded the map, carefully, and put it back in the case, and buckled the strap. Her hands were not quite steady and she did not care. ‘The Crown grant stops at the beck. Everything past it is what Vey means to have, and it's under his feet, and no one has ever written it down but a dead man and his apprentice.’
‘You've got it written down now,’ Ash said. He put his hat back on. ‘What do you want to do?’

Wren looked at the black mouth and the water coming out of it and the hill above going up into the fog, and she thought about the clerk's pen stopping in Harrowgate, and Rafe's grey-coated man at every door in Carrow, and the day after tomorrow.
‘I want to go down and find something to eat,’ she said, ‘and then I want to lay it before the Assize.’

scenes.title: The Assize

beats: Wren lays Edric’s survey before Magistrate Ide at the Carrow Assize.
Gale stands up to contest the claim on the Warden’s behalf and demands to see what the survey shows.
Ide reads the survey in private, refuses Gale, and seals the claim in Edric’s name and Wren’s.

paragraphs: They came down off the fell in the middle of the morning with the fog still on them, and Wren's boots squelched at every step along the causeway into Carrow. The bell in the abbey tower was ringing for the third hour. Carts stood jammed nose to tail in the market square, and the crowd had the particular noise of a place that has been full for three days: wool men with their hats pushed back, fell men in patched coats, a lawyer from the south in a black gown standing on the steps of the Wheatsheaf with a pipe in his mouth.

Ash took Cinder to the farrier's end of the square. Wren went up the abbey lane with the case under her arm, past the almshouse and the wall of the churchyard, to a low door in the north transept where two clerks sat at a trestle with a book open between them.
‘The Assize?’

The older clerk looked her over without interest. ‘Sits in the chapter house. It sits at ten and it rises when it’s done, and it’s been done since dinner yesterday. You’re late for today. Come back tomorrow.’
‘It sits tomorrow?’
‘It sits tomorrow. What is it?’
‘A survey,’ Wren said. ‘To be laid in the name of Edric Rone of Linmouth, sworn surveyor, and Wren Hollis, his apprentice.’

The clerk’s pen hovered. He wrote something down. He said, ‘Wait there,’ and went in through the door, and he was gone long enough that Wren had time to count the pigeons on the roof twice and to hear the market bell strike the half hour.
When he came back he held the door for her and said, ‘Magistrate will hear you now. He has the morning empty. Bring the instrument and the books.’

The chapter house was long and cold and smelled of stone and old wax. Light came in thin from three windows on the north side. A long table stood across the upper end with four men behind it, and the middle chair was occupied by a man of sixty-five or so with a dry brown face and a woollen gown over his coat, and he was reading a paper and did not look up when she came in.
The clerk set a chair for her on the near side of the table. The other three men looked at her and then at the case. The magistrate finished his paper, put it down, and looked at her.
‘You are Wren Hollis.’
‘Yes, sir.’
‘Of Linmouth. Apprentice to Edric Rone, sworn surveyor of that place.’

‘Six years, sir. He died three weeks ago this Friday. I have his last survey here, of Carrow Fell, finished the day he died, in his hand, with his seal and his field books, and I carried it from Linmouth to lay it before you before the Assize rises.’

The magistrate turned his hand over on the table, palm up, which she took for the asking. She unbuckled the strap and set the case on the table and opened it: the maps rolled in their linen, the field books stacked and tied with twine, the tin box with the seal in it. She laid them out in order, and put the last field book open at the final page, where the figures ran past the beck and the word *silver* stood underlined twice.
One of the other men leaned in to look. The magistrate did not. He said, ‘Read me the substance of it.’

‘The old lead workings on the north side of the fell, sir. The levels run a mile and a half past the second beck, bearing north by east from the second cairn. The Crown grant stops at the beck. Everything past it is unsurveyed, and it’s in his hand and mine, and I want it entered on the record in his name and mine.’

The magistrate put his hand on the map and turned it a quarter turn, as though he were reading a page upside down. He said nothing for a while. Then he said, ‘A dead man’s survey. You know what the court requires.’
‘I know what it requires, sir. The living hand swears he made it, and that I carried it, and that it is true as he left it. I’ll swear it.’

The magistrate looked at her burned hand where it lay on the table, and at her sleeve, and at her face. He said, ‘Wait outside. The clerk will call you when we want you again.’ And then, as she gathered up the case, the door at the back of the hall opened and a man came in with his hat off in his hand, a good grey coat ruined to the waist, and said, in a voice of easy courtesy:
‘Magistrate. Forgive me. I am come on the Warden’s behalf, and I have the Warden’s warrant, and I would ask the court to hear me before it makes any entry in this matter.’

Wren turned with the case in her arms. Gale stood in the doorway in his wet grey coat, and his hat in his hand, and he was looking at her and not at the magistrate, and he was smiling the way a man smiles when he has had a long ride and got there first.

Magistrate Ide did not smile. He said, ‘Master Gale. You have been to my clerk three times this week. I know who you are and whose you are. Say what you have to say, and be quick, because I have another matter at two.’

‘It is short,’ Gale said. He came in, and the clerk gave him a chair, and he sat down with his hat on his knee. ‘The Warden has an interest in the fell above this town. He has held the freeholds at its foot for two years and he holds the Crown grant of the minerals, and it is his intention to develop them for the good of the county. A survey of the fell, carried out by a man now dead, and offered here by an apprentice of six years, is a thing the Warden cannot see go on the record without knowing what is in it. I would ask the court to look at the survey itself, sir, and to let the Warden’s man see what it shows, in fairness, before any entry is made.’

‘It is not the Warden’s survey,’ Wren said. She had not meant to speak. Her voice came out flat and it carried in the stone room. ‘It’s Edric Rone’s, and it’s mine to lay. He knew what it shows. That’s why he drew it. If the Warden wants to see it, let him come and look at the record when it’s on the record, like any man.’

Gale turned his head and looked at her with what might have been kindness. ‘Mistress Hollis. I have never asked you what the survey shows. I don’t know to this hour what your master found up there. That is exactly my point. It may be gold, silver, lead, or chalk. The Warden is entitled to know what is sworn against his grant before it is sworn.’

‘He is entitled to nothing,’ the magistrate said, ‘until it is on the record, and then he is entitled to see the record like every other man in this room.’ He put his hand flat on the map. ‘Master Gale, you have made your application. I will consider the survey. In private. Not you. Not the Warden. Not the girl. The clerk and I. That is the practice of this court and has been for a hundred years. If it is what she says it is, it goes on the record in the names she gives, and the Warden may plead to it at the next Assize if he has anything to plead. Sit down and wait, or go home.’
Gale sat still for a moment. Then he put his hat on his knee, and said, ‘I will wait, sir,’ and he did not look at Wren again.

The clerk took the case, and the maps, and the field books, and the tin box with the seal, and carried them out through a side door into a small room off the hall. The magistrate followed him. The door closed. For a quarter of an hour the four of them sat in the chapter house and listened to the market bell and the noise of carts in the square. Wren sat with her hands folded in her lap. She could feel Gale across the room like a draught from a window.

The clerk came back and held the door, and the magistrate came out and sat down in his chair and put his hands on the table. He had a paper in front of him, and the paper had the seal on it, and the seal was in wax at the foot of the page, and it was his own seal, and the ink of the entry above it was dry enough to have taken the sand.

‘The survey of Carrow Fell,’ he said, ‘is entered on the record of this Assize in the name of Edric Rone, sworn surveyor of Linmouth, deceased, and Wren Hollis, his apprentice, of the same place, she having sworn this day that the said survey was made by the said Edric Rone, that she carried it from Linmouth, and that it is true as he left it. The instrument, the field books and the seal are filed with the roll. The entry stands. The Assize rises tomorrow, and the record closes with it.’ He looked at Gale. ‘Master Gale, you may tell the Warden that he may inspect the record at any time before the Assize rises, and that he may plead to it at the next. Good day to you.’
Gale stood. He put his hat on. He looked at Wren once, and his face had nothing on it at all, and then he went out through the back door and the clerk shut it behind him.

The magistrate turned to Wren. His dry face did not change. He said, ‘The seal is filed. You may have a copy of the entry made at the clerk’s table for two pence, if you want one. I would, in your place. Tomorrow is the last day. If you have anything else to put before me, put it before me then.’ He gathered his papers and stood, and the other three men stood with him.
Wren got out of her chair. Her legs were not quite steady, and she stood a moment with her hand on the back of it.
‘Thank you, sir,’ she said.
Outside, the bell was ringing for noon. Ash was waiting at the foot of the lane with Cinder, and when he saw her face he took his hat off.

scenes.title: The road out of Carrow

beats: They ride out of Carrow in the morning, the sealed claim safe.
Bryn turns her cart for Harrowgate and they part with rough affection.
Wren and Ash ride on together towards the coast.

paragraphs: They left Carrow by the north gate at six, before the market filled, with the fog still caught in the steep streets and the abbey bell striking the hour behind them. Wren rode Cinder at a walk, her left arm through the rein, the copy of the entry folded flat inside her jumper over the letter. Two pence it had cost, at the clerk's table, and the clerk had sanded it and blown the sand off and handed it to her without looking up.
