She had read it twice in the lamplight of the Wheatsheaf and once more at first light. *The survey of Carrow Fell, entered in the names of Edric Rone, sworn surveyor of Linmouth, deceased, and Wren Hollis, his apprentice, of the same place.* The words did not change, however many times she read them.

Bryn's cart stood in the square with the tailgate down and the horse already in the shafts, and Bryn was up on the bed of it, shifting the last of the dyed cloth with her boot. She had her pipe lit and her leather apron on over a coat that had dried stiff and grey.
‘You want the bale moved, you move it yourself,’ she said, without turning round. ‘I'm not stopping to be thanked.’
‘I wasn't going to thank you,’ Wren said.

‘Good.’ Bryn jumped down, and the cart rocked. She looked at Wren for a moment, unhurried, the way she looked at a shoe before she took it off. ‘Shoe's paid. That's the whole of it. Your name's not in my mouth at Harrowgate and it won't be at Carrow either, and if my brother hears of me from a Warden's man I'll know who told him.’
‘He won't hear it from me.’

‘No,’ Bryn said. ‘He won't.’ She spat on her hand and held it out, and Wren took it, and the grip was dry and hard as a harness ring. Then Bryn turned to Ash, who had come up leading Cinder, and she looked at his face a long time, at the thin pink line under the eye.
‘You'll be at Drake's Bottom by Michaelmas,’ she said.
‘I might.’

‘You might be dead by Michaelmas. It's the same to me which.’ She reached up and took hold of his collar and pulled his head down and knocked her forehead against his, once, hard enough to be heard across the square, and let him go. ‘Your mother's people were all fools,’ she said. ‘You take after the other side.’
‘Which side is that?’

‘Mine.’ She climbed up onto the seat and gathered the reins and clicked her tongue, and the cart rolled off across the cobbles towards the south gate, and she did not look back, and neither of them said anything until she was out of the square and the noise of the market had closed over her.

They rode north out of the gate with the last of the fog burning off the roofs behind them. The road ran down off the town shoulder and levelled along the flat green land, with the fell on the left going back into cloud and the river somewhere out of sight on the right, and the salt smell coming up on the wind, faint, and then not faint.

‘She'll be at Harrowgate in four days,’ Ash said. ‘She'll have the salt fish sold in three and the cloth before that, and she'll be sitting in Sela's taproom by Friday telling them all about a girl she never met.’

Her arm ached under the grease and the fresh linen, the ache going up from the wrist to the elbow and settling there like a hand held over it. She had slept most of the night, on a bench by the fire in the Wheatsheaf, with the case gone from under her head and the entry in her jumper, and had woken not knowing for a moment where she was.

He had his collar up and his hands in his armpits and his hat down against the wind off the flat land. ‘I'll see you to Haldon Bridge,’ he said. ‘There's a fair at Fallow Cross the week after next. If you're walking the levels on that fell you'll want a man to carry the staff and count the paces and tell you when you've counted wrong, and I know when you've counted wrong, I've watched you do it twice.’
‘Once,’ Wren said.

‘Twice. You lost the cairn in the fog and you'd have walked off the crag.’ He looked sideways at her. ‘And you'll have the mare back by then, and the mare's yours, and I've no claim on her. I'm not asking for wages. I'm asking for the walking.’

Wren looked out over the flat green land. There was a line of willows along a drain, and beyond them a village with a squat tower, and beyond that the country going on and on, all of it somebody's to survey, all of it held by some paper in some box in some room.
‘You'll have to be told what to do,’ she said.

The road bent north-east and began to climb a little, and the smell of salt came stronger, and far off to the right, past the flat land, there was a grey line that was not land and was not sky, and Wren looked at it and knew it for what it was, and knew that in a day and a half the salt road would bring them round to the coast and down by the Linn, and that Oskar Venn's punt would be there or not, and that beyond it, up the valley, there was a farm with a dun mare in a paddock and a woman with a bucket who wanted two shillings.

Four pence in her pocket, and the two pence for the copy gone from it, and the account in her head ran out: two shillings to the farm, and Thistle, and then the fell, and the drain above the second beck that Edric had never surveyed, and a man to carry the staff.
‘You'll need a coat,’ she said. ‘Before the fair. You can't walk the fell in that one.’
‘It's a good coat.’
‘It's a rag. It's got a knife-hole in the collar and the collar's the only part that was ever whole.’
‘It's dry,’ Ash said. ‘That's all I ask of a coat.’

They rode on north, and the fog lifted off the fell behind them and lay along the top of it in a white band, and the sun came up over the flat land, thin and low and cold, and neither of them said anything else for a mile or more.
